196089.long_answer:
Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease is most often produced by a 1.4- to 1.5-Mb tandem duplication containing the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17p11.2-p12 (CMT1A).  Other, far less common CMT subtypes are caused by point mutations or small indels in more than 100 different genes scattered on many chromosomes, but the 17p11.2 duplication remains the prototypic chromosomal abnormality associated with the disorder.

The very rare "Absent tibia–polydactyly–arachnoid cyst" syndrome has been reported in only a few families.  In those reports the underlying structural chromosome change was NOT the 17p11.2 PMP22 duplication; instead the patients carried rearrangements involving an entirely different chromosomal region (e.g., interstitial deletions on the long arm of chromosome 6).  Thus the cytogenetic abnormality responsible for this limb/CNS malformation syndrome is distinct from the duplication that produces the common form of CMT.

Because the two conditions are associated with mutations or rearrangements on different chromosomes, they are not caused by the same chromosomal abnormality.

442406.long_answer: Linkage studies of the autosomal-recessive condition known as familial multiple intestinal atresia—characterised by atresia occurring at many sites throughout both the small and large intestines—have mapped the responsible locus to the long arm of chromosome 19 (19q13), demonstrating that the causative gene is located on chromosome 19.

305681.long_answer: One major form of hereditary lymphedema, Milroy disease (hereditary lymphedema type I), is indeed most often caused by heterozygous mutations in the FLT4 gene that encodes vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-3 (VEGFR-3). However, the disorder is historically linked to the American physician William Milroy, who first described the familial condition in 1892. Rudolf Virchow, although an influential pathologist known for eponyms such as Virchow’s node and Virchow’s triad, has no specific historical or scientific association with hereditary lymphedema. Because the second part of the statement is incorrect, the overall statement is considered false.

198351.long_answer: The rare skeletal disorders Jansen metaphyseal and Blomstrand chondrodysplasia are caused by gain- or loss-of-function mutations in the parathyroid hormone 1 receptor (PTH1R), a class B G protein-coupled receptor. PTH1R normally mediates PTH/PTHrP signalling that delays endochondral ossification; when it is mutated this regulation fails, producing premature or ectopic bone formation and markedly accelerated skeletal maturation. Thus, the GPCR mutated in these disorders with abnormal ossification and advanced bone age is the parathyroid hormone 1 receptor.

590061.long_answer: Yes. Smith–Magenis syndrome is most commonly produced by an interstitial micro-deletion of chromosome 17p11.2 that removes the RAI1 gene; point mutations in RAI1 within this same band can also cause the disorder. Potocki-Lupski syndrome is the reciprocal genomic disorder: a micro-duplication of the identical 17p11.2 segment that includes RAI1. Thus both syndromes arise from pathogenic copy-number alterations affecting the 17p11.2 chromosomal region.

303803.long_answer:
Carpenter syndrome is an autosomal-recessive craniosynostosis–polysyndactyly disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in genes such as RAB23 or MEGF8.  

The entity usually referred to as “cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome” (sometimes called acro-/cephalopolysyndactyly type I) has been reported to follow autosomal-dominant transmission, with many cases arising from a single heterozygous mutation and showing vertical transmission in affected families.  

Because cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome is inherited in an autosomal-dominant manner, whereas Carpenter syndrome is inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner, they do not share the same inheritance pattern.

758793.long_answer: Cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita (CMTC) is a congenital vascular malformation that is usually apparent on the skin at birth or within the first days of life, making it typically recognized shortly after birth. Glaucoma, by contrast, most commonly presents later in childhood or adulthood (except for the rarer primary congenital form), so it is not generally detected immediately after birth.

160759.long_answer:
Pyle disease (metaphyseal dysplasia, Pyle type; OMIM #265900) is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in the SFRP4 gene (Secreted Frizzled-Related Protein 4).  Independent of its role in bone development, SFRP4 modulates Wnt signalling in pancreatic islets and adipose tissue.  Multiple human and experimental studies have reported that:
• Circulating SFRP4 concentrations are significantly elevated years before the clinical onset of type 2 diabetes and predict future diabetes risk (e.g., Mahdi et al., Nature Medicine 2012; prospective cohort follow-up studies).
• Over-expression or recombinant SFRP4 impairs glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in isolated human and murine β-cells, while Sfrp4 knockout improves β-cell function in mice.
• Common genetic variants near or within SFRP4 show nominal association with fasting glucose and type 2 diabetes in several genome-wide association and candidate-gene studies.
Although SFRP4 mutations do not cause monogenic diabetes, the gene/protein is nevertheless regarded in the endocrinology literature as a biomarker and mechanistic contributor to type 2 diabetes pathophysiology.  Therefore, the gene that causes Pyle disease is also linked—through biomarker, functional, and genetic evidence—to diabetes.

352943.long_answer: Pyle disease (metaphyseal dysplasia, Pyle type) is caused by recessive loss-of-function mutations in the SFRP4 gene (Secreted Frizzled-Related Protein 4). The SFRP4 gene is mapped to chromosome 7p14. Hence, the gene responsible for Pyle disease is located on chromosome 7.

213436.long_answer: Mutations in the ITM2B gene, situated on chromosome 13q14, cause Familial British and Familial Danish dementias. These disorders exhibit cerebral amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles that closely resemble the neuropathology of Alzheimer’s disease, linking ITM2B to Alzheimer-like dementias.

189121.long_answer: Familial British dementia is caused by a stop-codon mutation in the ITM2B (BRI2) gene, which is situated on the long arm of chromosome 13 (13q14).

976949.long_answer: The gene encoding alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)—the principal plasma protein made by the fetal yolk sac and liver and measured in maternal serum to screen for neural tube defects like spina bifida—resides on human chromosome 4 (long arm, region q13).

875070.long_answer: Mitochondrial membrane protein–associated neurodegeneration (MPAN) is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the nuclear gene C19orf12.  Subsequent clinical reports showed that the phenotypic spectrum of C19orf12 mutations is broader than classic MPAN with brain-iron accumulation: several families have been described in which the predominant presentation is very-early-onset optic atrophy together with spinocerebellar degeneration/ataxia (often accompanied by spasticity or axonal neuropathy) and little or no iron detectable on brain MRI.  Molecular analysis in these patients identified exactly the same gene—C19orf12—that had previously been implicated in MPAN.  Thus, the syndrome of early-onset optic atrophy with spinocerebellar degeneration is indeed associated with mutations in the gene already known to cause mitochondrial membrane protein-associated neurodegeneration, confirming a shared genetic basis.

321692.long_answer: Type I tyrosinemia is caused by biallelic mutations in the fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase (FAH) gene. The FAH gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 15 (cytogenetic band 15q23-q25).

332575.long_answer: Rosenthal fibers are intracellular aggregates composed largely of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). Mutations in the GFAP gene drive their accumulation, as seen in Alexander disease and certain astrocytomas. The GFAP gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 17 (17q21), establishing chromosome 17 as the genomic location linked to Rosenthal-fiber production.

510654.long_answer: Familial amyloid polyneuropathy is most commonly caused by pathogenic variants in the transthyretin (TTR) gene. The human TTR gene is located at cytogenetic band 18q12.1 on chromosome 18. Chromosome 18 spans roughly 80 million base pairs, matching the size stated in the question, and thus carries the gene responsible for this hereditary amyloid neuropathy.

521164.long_answer: Pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase, BCHE) deficiency is classically inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner. The BCHE gene is located on chromosome 3q26; affected individuals are typically homozygous (or compound heterozygous) for loss-of-function variants, while heterozygotes have only a partial reduction in enzyme activity. Because two defective alleles are required for the clinically significant deficiency, it is not transmitted by a dominant allele. Therefore, the statement that pseudocholinesterase deficiency is caused by a dominant allele on an autosomal chromosome is incorrect.

307739.long_answer: The RPS6KA3 gene lies on Xp22.12 and encodes the RSK2 serine/threonine kinase, an effector of the MAPK/ERK pathway that helps regulate cell growth, proliferation and differentiation. Loss-of-function mutations in RPS6KA3 produce Coffin-Lowry syndrome, an X-linked disorder that was described independently by Grange S. Coffin in 1966 and Robert B. Lowry in 1971, hence the disease’s eponym.

127417.long_answer: Intellectual disability in Arakawa Syndrome II occurs together with a characteristic constellation of other congenital anomalies – such as short stature, cranio-facial dysmorphism and skeletal abnormalities – that collectively define the disorder. Because the cognitive impairment is one component of a broader, clinically recognisable syndrome rather than an isolated finding, it is classified as syndromic intellectual disability according to current medical genetics consensus.

390910.long_answer: A single mildly enlarged (13 mm) axillary lymph node lacking a fatty hilum is a nonspecific imaging finding. Loss of the fatty hilum can be seen with many benign or malignant conditions—including reactive hyperplasia, infections, lymphoma, metastatic carcinoma, and numerous leukemias—but it is not characteristic or diagnostic for any one disorder. T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL) typically presents with marked peripheral blood lymphocytosis, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, skin lesions, and often generalized (not isolated) lymphadenopathy. Definitive diagnosis requires hematologic studies (blood smear, flow cytometry, cytogenetics), not sonographic features of a single node. Therefore, the presence of a 13 mm axillary lymph node without a fatty hilum does not specifically suggest T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia.

520726.long_answer: Men who are insensitive to follicle-stimulating hormone (because of FSH-β subunit deficiency or inactivating mutations in the FSH receptor) generally show only the consequences of absent FSH signalling on the Sertoli cells and spermatogenesis. Leydig cells, which produce testosterone, are stimulated primarily by luteinising hormone (LH), a pathway that is intact in these patients. Consequently, serum LH and Leydig-cell function remain normal, and circulating testosterone concentrations are usually within the normal adult male range, permitting normal virilisation. Numerous clinical reports of men with FSHβ or FSHR mutations describe azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia with normal testosterone levels. Therefore, the scientifically accepted consensus is that testosterone levels are typically normal in men with FSH insensitivity.

533612.long_answer: Postencephalitic parkinsonism developed in survivors of the 1919–1930 encephalitis lethargica epidemic. Compared with idiopathic Parkinson’s disease, it typically began at a younger age and characteristically lacked the classic pill-rolling resting tremor.

648793.long_answer:
Several genes located on chromosome 14 are known to cause a syndromic combination of severe eye malformations (microphthalmia, anophthalmia, structural disorganization of the globe) together with limb defects when they are deleted or carry loss-of-function variants. The best-documented examples are:

• BMP4 (14q22-q23): Heterozygous BMP4 loss-of-function variants or microdeletions encompassing BMP4 produce microphthalmia/anophthalmia, anterior segment dysgenesis, and a spectrum of limb anomalies such as polydactyly, syndactyly, or brachydactyly.

• OTX2 (14q22.3): Pathogenic variants or deletions of OTX2 lead to severe ocular malformations (anophthalmia/microphthalmia, coloboma) and, in a subset of patients, limb anomalies or other skeletal findings.

Therefore, a deficiency (haploinsufficiency) of a gene on chromosome 14 can indeed account for the presentation of unusually small, structurally disorganized eyes together with limb anomalies. The statement is consistent with current genetic and clinical evidence.

181257.long_answer: Mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD) is an autosomal-recessive autoinflammatory disease due to pathogenic variants in the MVK gene. The MVK gene encodes the enzyme mevalonate kinase, which catalyzes an early step in the cholesterol/isoprenoid biosynthetic pathway. Mutations in MVK reduce or abolish the activity of this enzyme, leading to the clinical spectrum that includes hyper-IgD syndrome and mevalonic aciduria. Thus, the disorder is indeed caused by a defective gene whose loss-of-function results in a deficiency of the mevalonate kinase enzyme.

353225.long_answer: Macrosomia (generalized over-growth), macroglossia (enlarged tongue) and hemihyperplasia/hemihypertrophy are cardinal clinical manifestations of Beckwith–Wiedemann spectrum and other isolated over-growth disorders. These conditions are well known cancer-predisposition syndromes: children who exhibit any of these over-growth features have a markedly increased risk of developing embryonal tumours, most commonly Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma), as well as hepatoblastoma and others. Consequently, current pediatric oncology guidelines recommend periodic abdominal ultrasonography for Wilms tumour surveillance in patients with Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome or isolated hemihyperplasia. Therefore, it is scientifically established that individuals showing macrosomia, macroglossia or hemihyperplasia can indeed also present with Wilms tumour.

261207.long_answer: Neonatal diabetes mellitus (onset before 6 months of age) is a monogenic disorder most frequently produced by heterozygous (autosomal-dominant) mutations in genes that impair insulin secretion or production. The commonest examples are activating mutations in KCNJ11 and ABCC8, which encode the two subunits (Kir6.2 and SUR1) of the pancreatic ATP-sensitive K⁺ channel, and heterozygous mutations in the INS gene that lead to misfolded insulin. These mutations are inherited in an autosomal-dominant manner and directly disrupt the β-cell’s ability to produce or secrete insulin, resulting in hyperglycaemia in the newborn period. Although some rarer forms of neonatal diabetes follow autosomal-recessive inheritance (e.g., mutations in EIF2AK3, GCK, PDX1), the well-established and most common mechanisms are indeed autosomal-dominant mutations that interfere with insulin production/secretion. Therefore, the statement is consistent with established scientific consensus.

953189.long_answer: The chromosomal anomaly in which a genetic male has one extra X chromosome is Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY). One of the core pathophysiologic features of Klinefelter syndrome is primary testicular failure, which results in decreased production of testosterone (an androgen) and relatively increased conversion of androgens to estrogens by aromatase in adipose tissue. The consequent low-androgen / high-estrogen milieu underlies many of the clinical manifestations: small testes, reduced facial and body hair, gynecomastia, tall eunuchoid habitus, diminished muscle mass, decreased libido, and infertility. Because these symptoms are directly linked to the imbalance of androgens and estrogens, estrogens and androgens are indeed associated with the symptomatology of males who carry an extra X chromosome.

234120.long_answer: The lethal form of Tetra-amelia syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the RSPO2 gene, an essential activator of canonical Wnt/β-catenin signalling during embryogenesis. RSPO2 is required for both limb-bud outgrowth and the initiation of lung bud formation; when it is mutated, the lungs fail to develop, leading to perinatal lethality. In humans the RSPO2 gene is situated on chromosome 8 (band 8q23.1), so the responsible gene—and therefore the syndrome-causing mutations—are located on human chromosome 8.

707794.long_answer: Proteus syndrome is a mosaic overgrowth disorder caused by somatic-activating mutations in the AKT1 gene. Because the abnormal overgrowth, adipose dysregulation, connective-tissue nevi, and vascular/lymphatic malformations can occur in almost any anatomic region, the genitourinary tract—including the scrotum and testes—may be affected. Reported manifestations in male patients have included paratesticular lipomatosis, hemangiomas or lymphatic malformations of the scrotum, asymmetric testicular enlargement, and, more rarely, benign or malignant testicular tumors. Any of these lesions can present clinically as a palpable “lump” in the testis or scrotum. Local overgrowth, vascular congestion, torsion of an enlarged epididymis, or tumor growth can also produce sharp pain or a dull, dragging ache in the lower abdomen or scrotal area. Therefore, it is within the recognized clinical spectrum of Proteus syndrome for an affected individual to notice a testicular/scrotal mass accompanied by pain or discomfort.

280793.long_answer: Calcinosis cutis refers to dystrophic or metastatic deposition of insoluble calcium salts within skin and sub-cutaneous tissues. It is the “C” of the CREST variant of limited systemic scleroderma, presenting as firm nodules or plaques of calcium. Similar soft-tissue calcium deposits can also develop in other settings that disturb calcium–phosphate balance or cause tissue injury, such as chronic kidney failure, hyperparathyroidism, or local infection.

314628.long_answer: Asphyxiating thoracic dysplasia (also called Jeune syndrome or short-rib thoracic dysplasia) is genetically heterogeneous. Among the many ciliary genes in which pathogenic variants have been documented, several are located on chromosome 2. Well-established examples include WDR35 (IFT121) at 2p24 and TTC21B (IFT139) at 2q24.3. Pathogenic mutations in these genes are known, through multiple independent studies and OMIM entries, to cause short-rib thoracic dysplasia/Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dysplasia. Therefore, mutations in genes situated on chromosome 2 are indeed associated with asphyxiating thoracic dysplasia.

455108.long_answer:
The rare inherited bone-growth disorder first described by Jeune in 1955 is Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy (also called Jeune syndrome). Multiple genes have been shown to cause this ciliopathy, including IFT80, DYNC2H1, WDR35, WDR19, TTC21B, IFT140, IFT172, CSPP1 and several others. The WD-repeat gene on chromosome 2 that is definitively implicated is WDR35, not WDR12. 

WDR12 (WD repeat domain 12) is a component of the PeBoW complex involved in ribosome biogenesis; to date it has not been associated with Jeune syndrome or any other skeletal dysplasia in the medical genetics literature. Therefore, the statement that the WDR12 gene on chromosome 2 is implicated in causing the disorder is not supported by established scientific consensus.

296800.long_answer: Ascariasis is the intestinal disease produced by the roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides. The parasite survives in the human gut by secreting potent inhibitors of host digestive enzymes (e.g., serine-protease and cysteine-protease inhibitors), which block enzymes such as trypsin and chymotrypsin, allowing the worm to resist degradation and establish infection.

339025.long_answer: The gene that occupies chromosome 6p21.3 from base-pair 33,238,446 to 33,268,222 is COL11A2 (collagen, type XI, alpha 2). Pathogenic variants in COL11A2 cause Stickler syndrome type 3 (also called the non-ocular form). By definition, this subtype lacks the characteristic eye manifestations (high myopia, retinal detachment, cataracts, etc.) seen in the classic COL2A1- and COL11A1-related forms of Stickler syndrome. Therefore, mutations in this gene do not affect the eyes in Stickler syndrome.

334602.long_answer: Autosomal-recessive loss-of-function mutations in the PYCR1 gene, which encodes the mitochondrial NAD(P)H-dependent pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase that converts pyrroline-5-carboxylate to proline, produce a cutis laxa/progeroid disorder that clinically resembles De Barsy syndrome.

655628.long_answer: The JAK2 V617F point mutation (valine-to-phenylalanine at codon 617) occurs in the Janus kinase 2 gene, a non-receptor tyrosine kinase that transduces signals from type I and type II cytokine receptor families. This gain-of-function mutation constitutively activates JAK-STAT signaling and is found in about 50–60 % of patients with essential thrombocythemia, making it the mutation most commonly linked to the disease.

559693.long_answer: Porphyrias are a group of inherited (or occasionally acquired) metabolic disorders caused by mutations that reduce the activity of one of the eight enzymes in the heme-biosynthetic pathway. Heme is the iron-containing prosthetic group essential for hemoglobin and thus for oxygen transport in blood. When an enzyme in this pathway is deficient, porphyrin precursors accumulate, producing the characteristic neurovisceral or cutaneous symptoms. Hippocrates provided the earliest clinical descriptions of such attacks, making porphyrias one of the oldest recognized genetic disease groups.

597959.long_answer: Multiple system atrophy is an α-synucleinopathy in which glial cytoplasmic inclusions are packed with aggregated α-synuclein. The α-synuclein protein is encoded by the SNCA gene; hence, SNCA is the gene whose product forms the characteristic inclusions in MSA.

191988.long_answer: The CFTR gene responsible for cystic fibrosis is situated on chromosome 7 at band q31.2. Pathogenic mutations in CFTR lead to the multisystem disorder cystic fibrosis, whereas campomelic dysplasia is linked to mutations in the SOX9 gene on chromosome 17. Therefore, the disorder associated with the 7q31.2 locus is cystic fibrosis.

264925.long_answer: Trimethadione is an anticonvulsant; teratogenicity from this class of antiepileptic drugs (e.g., trimethadione, valproate, carbamazepine) is well known to cause neural-tube–closure defects. The prototypical neural-tube defect linked to these anticonvulsants is spina bifida, making it the birth defect associated with the same medication class that produces fetal trimethadione syndrome.

314081.long_answer: Jansen’s metaphyseal chondrodysplasia is caused by activating (constitutively active) mutations in the parathyroid hormone/parathyroid-hormone–related-peptide receptor gene (PTHR1). PTHR1 encodes a G protein-coupled receptor that belongs to class B of the GPCR superfamily, historically called the “secretin family” of GPCRs. Members of this family share a characteristic long N-terminal extracellular domain and include receptors for secretin, glucagon, calcitonin, and related peptide hormones. Because PTHR1 is a bona-fide secretin-family (class B) GPCR, the gene responsible for Jansen’s metaphyseal chondrodysplasia is indeed a member of the secretin family of G protein-coupled receptors.

701727.long_answer:
Nociplastic pain is defined by the International Association for the Study of Pain as pain that arises from altered nociception in the absence of clear evidence of tissue damage or a lesion of the somatosensory system. The neural substrate concerned is therefore the somatosensory (nociceptive) system—i.e., the sensory pathways that detect and process noxious stimuli in both the peripheral and central nervous systems. 

In neuroanatomy, the functional subdivision into “somatic” and “autonomic” applies to the motor (efferent) portion of the peripheral nervous system: the somatic nervous system controls voluntary skeletal muscle, whereas the autonomic nervous system regulates involuntary visceral functions (sympathetic, parasympathetic, and enteric). The sensory/somatosensory system, which includes nociceptive afferents, is not categorized into somatic vs. autonomic divisions in this way. Consequently, the part of the nervous system implicated in nociplastic pain is not described as being split into somatic and autonomic divisions.

Therefore, the statement that the nervous system component associated with nociplastic pain “divides into somatic and autonomic divisions” is not supported by established anatomical or pain-science consensus.

289582.long_answer: Schindler disease is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the lysosomal exoglycosidase α-N-acetylgalactosaminidase. In humans, this enzyme is produced from the NAGA gene located on chromosome 22q13. Mutations that abolish or markedly reduce NAGA activity lead to accumulation of glycopeptides and glycolipids, producing the clinical manifestations of Schindler disease.

673283.long_answer: Stickler syndrome involves mutations in the COL2A1 gene encoding type II collagen. Type II collagen is the predominant structural protein of the eye’s vitreous body (vitreous humor); defects in this collagen therefore disrupt the integrity of the vitreous, leading to the ocular manifestations characteristic of Stickler syndrome.

583241.long_answer: Stickler syndrome is caused by mutations in genes encoding collagen (especially type II and XI collagens). Proper collagen synthesis requires hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues, a reaction that depends on vitamin C (ascorbic acid) as an essential co-factor. Therefore, vitamin C is the vitamin crucial for synthesizing the collagen that is defective in Stickler syndrome.

474223.long_answer: Juvenile (X-linked) retinoschisis is caused by mutations in the RS1 (retinoschisin) gene. RS1 is situated on the short arm of the X chromosome at band Xp22.1-p22.2, so the pathogenic variants that produce retinoschisis reside on the X chromosome.

595243.long_answer: Both conditions are universally recognized as genetic disorders. Cystic fibrosis results from pathogenic, usually recessively inherited, variants in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7; disruption of CFTR‐mediated chloride transport underlies the characteristic pulmonary, pancreatic and other systemic manifestations. Campomelic dysplasia is a severe skeletal dysplasia caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or chromosomal rearrangements involving the SOX9 gene on chromosome 17; although most cases arise de novo, the disorder is nonetheless genetic because the clinical phenotype stems directly from germline alteration of a specific gene. Therefore, according to current biomedical consensus, both CF and CMD are properly categorized as genetic disorders.

310034.long_answer: Mutations in the CFTR gene, identified in 1989, disrupt the function of the CFTR protein—an ABC transporter-class chloride and bicarbonate ion channel present on epithelial cell membranes. Loss or reduction of CFTR-mediated ion transport dehydrates airway surface liquid, producing thick, sticky mucus that cannot be cleared effectively. This defect underlies the autosomal-recessive genetic disorder cystic fibrosis, characterized by chronic lung infections, pancreatic insufficiency, and other systemic complications.

102914.long_answer: Peutz–Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is an inherited condition transmitted in an autosomal-dominant fashion. The great majority of cases are caused by pathogenic variants in the STK11/LKB1 gene, which is located on chromosome 19p13.3—an autosome (non-sex chromosome). Therefore, PJS is indeed a genetic disorder whose causative gene variants reside on a non-sex chromosome.

100063.long_answer: After the original English sibship described by Jancar, only two additional kindreds have been published: one Belgian family (siblings reported by Van Broeckhoven et al.) and one Israeli family (siblings reported by Ben-Neriah et al.). Thus, besides England, the countries where familial cases of intellectual disability-spasticity-ectrodactyly (Jancar) syndrome have been documented are Belgium and Israel.

873298.long_answer: George Miller Beard, the 19th-century American neurologist who coined the diagnosis “neurasthenia,” recommended a combination of physical and somatic measures—most famously electrical stimulation (faradic and galvanic currents), nutritious diet, massage, tonics, and periods of rest. In contrast, the Japanese psychiatrist Shōma Morita (originator of Morita Therapy in the early 20th century) treated neurasthenic patients with a staged psychotherapeutic program that began with several days of strict bed-rest and isolation, followed by graded occupational activity and counseling aimed at accepting unpleasant feelings. Although both men included a brief initial rest period, Morita’s method was essentially a behavioral-psychological regimen, whereas Beard’s approach centered on electrotherapy and physiological tonics. Because the therapeutic programs they advocated differ fundamentally in rationale and procedure, Beard and Morita did not propose the same treatment for neurasthenia.

343060.long_answer: ARC syndrome is caused by mutations in the VPS33B gene. VPS33B encodes a vacuolar-trafficking protein that is classified within the Sec1/Munc18 (SM) family of proteins, a conserved group that regulates SNARE-dependent membrane fusion events in vesicle transport.

592016.long_answer: Mucolipidosis type I (sialidosis) is one of the lysosomal storage disorders. The clinical picture it produces—coarse-facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, developmental delay, bone dysplasia, cherry-red macula, myoclonus, etc.—is not pathognomonic for ML I; very similar constellations of signs are seen in several other inborn errors of metabolism, particularly other lysosomal storage diseases such as the mucopolysaccharidoses (e.g., Hurler, Hunter), mucolipidosis II/III (I-cell disease), GM1/GM2 gangliosidoses, and some oligosaccharidoses. Therefore the symptoms of ML I do indeed also occur in other inherited metabolic disorders.

528453.long_answer: Glycogen storage disease type Ib results from deficiency of the glucose-6-phosphate translocase, a membrane protein that forms a selective channel shuttling glucose-6-phosphate between the endoplasmic reticulum lumen and the cytosol. This translocase is encoded by the SLC37A4 gene; mutations in SLC37A4 abolish or reduce its function, leading to the metabolic and neutropenic manifestations of GSD-Ib.

988380.long_answer: GM1 gangliosidosis is estimated to occur in roughly 1 in 100,000–200,000 live births, whereas lysosomal storage diseases as a whole occur in about 1 in 5,000–7,700 live births. Because a higher denominator means lower frequency, the much rarer GM1 gangliosidosis has the lower incidence compared with the combined lysosomal storage disease group.

520077.long_answer: Presbyopia is the age-related loss of the eye’s ability to change the lens power for near focus (accommodation). A constricted pupil—such as in bright sunlight—acts like a small aperture in a camera: it raises the eye’s effective f-number (focal ratio), which increases depth of field and depth of focus. With a greater depth of focus, the retinal image stays acceptably sharp over a wider range of object distances even though the lens can no longer change shape adequately. This pinhole effect does not restore accommodation, but it does reduce the blur that presbyopic eyes would otherwise experience at near, making the condition less noticeable in bright light. Therefore, the statement is consistent with established optical and clinical knowledge.

844232.long_answer: Aromatase excess syndrome is a very rare condition produced by gain-of-function rearrangements that massively overexpress the CYP19A1 (aromatase) gene, resulting in abnormally high estrogen levels. The CYP19A1 gene is located on chromosome 15q21.2; therefore, chromosome 15 is the chromosome that carries the mutated, overexpressed gene responsible for this syndrome.

940867.long_answer: Myhre syndrome is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the SMAD4 gene. SMAD4 encodes a member of the SMAD family of intracellular signal-transducer proteins, which act as modulators of signalling by ligands of the transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) superfamily.

797267.long_answer: The ASPM gene, the most frequently mutated gene in autosomal-recessive primary microcephaly and composed of 28 exons coding for a large centrosomal protein, is mapped to chromosome 1q31. Hence, it resides on chromosome 1.

191200.long_answer: The β-glucuronidase (GUSB) gene, whose deficiency causes mucopolysaccharidosis type VII (Sly syndrome) with excessive glycosaminoglycan accumulation, is located on human chromosome 7 (region 7q11).

691881.long_answer: The autosomal-recessive disorder first reported by Albert Schinzel in 1979, now called acrocallosal (Schinzel) syndrome, is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the kinesin family member 7 gene (KIF7). KIF7 encodes a ciliary kinesin that modulates the Hedgehog signalling pathway by controlling GLI transcription factor activity; pathogenic variants in KIF7 disrupt this regulation, producing the characteristic craniofacial, limb and corpus callosum anomalies of the syndrome.

505903.long_answer: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is almost always caused by a recurrent activating mutation (most commonly c.617G>A; p.R206H) in the ACVR1 gene, also known as ALK2. The ACVR1 gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 2 (cytogenetic band 2q23-q24). Chromosome 2 is one of the 22 numbered human chromosomes that are classified as autosomes (i.e., chromosomes that are not sex chromosomes X or Y). Therefore, the chromosome harboring the FOP-causing gene is indeed an autosome, making the statement correct.

985734.long_answer: The hereditary form of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor gene (CSF2). CSF2 is situated in the cytokine gene cluster on the long arm of chromosome 5 at band q31, so the pathogenic mutation maps to the 5q31 region.

357263.long_answer: Mutations in the Atlastin-1 gene (symbol ATL1) are the well-established cause of Strumpell-Lorrain disease, also known as autosomal-dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia type 3A (HSP-SPG3A). ATL1 encodes a dynamin-like GTPase that mediates endoplasmic-reticulum membrane fusion; loss of its normal function leads to progressive spasticity and weakness predominantly in the lower limbs characteristic of this disorder.

267044.long_answer: Familial male-limited precocious puberty (FMPP, or testotoxicosis) was first reported by the Harvard endocrinologist Fuller Albright. Albright, a pioneer in endocrine disorders, was born on 12 January 1900; hence, the year of birth of the individual who first described FMPP is 1900.

523257.long_answer: The hormone implicated in hypoaldosteronism is aldosterone, the principal mineralocorticoid that regulates sodium and potassium balance. Aldosterone was first isolated and chemically characterized in 1953 by Simpson and Tait and colleagues, establishing its role in adrenal physiology and disorders such as hypoaldosteronism.

524865.long_answer: Both Dubin–Johnson syndrome and Rotor syndrome are hereditary disorders characterized by impaired hepatic handling of bilirubin that has already been conjugated within hepatocytes. Because the conjugation step is intact, the bilirubin accumulating in the bloodstream is predominantly conjugated (direct-reacting) bilirubin. Dubin–Johnson syndrome results from mutations in the canalicular transporter MRP2 (ABCC2), preventing efficient excretion of conjugated bilirubin into bile. Rotor syndrome involves defects in hepatic storage/re-uptake transporters (OATP1B1/OATP1B3), leading to leakage of conjugated bilirubin back into the blood. Clinically, both conditions therefore present with chronic, predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia while hepatic synthetic function and transaminases remain normal. This relationship is well established in hepatology literature, so the statement is correct.

526400.long_answer: The PNKD gene (formerly MR-1), whose mutations cause Paroxysmal Nonkinesigenic Dyskinesia, is alternatively spliced into several isoforms. The short isoform, designated PNKD-S, shows highest and predominant expression in the brain and other central nervous system tissues, whereas the long isoform is mainly found in peripheral tissues such as skeletal muscle. Therefore, the PNKD-S isoform is the one chiefly expressed in the CNS.

496452.long_answer: Albers-Schönberg disease, the classical autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type II, is caused by pathogenic mutations in the CLCN7 gene, which encodes the ClC-7 chloride/proton exchanger essential for acidification of the osteoclast resorption lacuna. Loss or reduction of ClC-7 function impairs osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, leading to the generalized increase in bone density characteristic of this disorder.

117819.long_answer: Mutations in the X-chromosomal T-box transcription factor gene TBX22 give rise to CPX syndrome (Cleft Palate, X-linked with or without ankyloglossia). This rare X-linked disorder is characterized by overt or submucous cleft palate often accompanied by tongue-tie (ankyloglossia). TBX22 is expressed in the developing palatal shelves and tongue; loss-of-function variants disrupt normal palatogenesis and tongue separation, producing the inherited cleft palate with ankyloglossia phenotype.

216561.long_answer: Roberts syndrome (also known as SC phocomelia) is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the ESCO2 gene. ESCO2 encodes an acetyltransferase required for proper sister-chromatid cohesion during cell division. Multiple linkage and positional-cloning studies have mapped ESCO2 to chromosome 8, band p21.1 (8p21.1). There is no evidence that Roberts syndrome is linked to a locus on chromosome 6, and 6q21.1 is not implicated in this disorder. Therefore, the statement that the gene associated with Roberts syndrome is located at 6q21.1 on chromosome 6 is incorrect.

687993.long_answer: Roberts syndrome is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the ESCO2 gene (Establishment of Sister Chromatid Cohesion N-acetyltransferase 2), which is mapped to cytogenetic band 8p21.1 on human chromosome 8.

281757.long_answer: Woodhouse-Sakati syndrome (OMIM #241080) is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in the gene DCAF17 (formerly C2orf37). Cellular and bioinformatic studies show that the DCAF17 protein contains two hydrophobic segments that span membrane bilayers and that the protein is anchored in the inner nuclear membrane/nuclear envelope while also extending into the nucleolus. Because the disease-causing gene product is an integral membrane protein of the nuclear envelope, it is classified as a nuclear transmembrane protein. Therefore, the statement is consistent with established scientific evidence.

933696.long_answer: Woodhouse–Sakati syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the DCAF17 gene (formerly C2orf37), which encodes a nuclear transmembrane protein. DCAF17 is situated at cytogenetic band 2q31.1 on chromosome 2.

256147.long_answer: Fanconi syndrome in infants and young children is most commonly produced by nephropathic cystinosis. This disorder results from loss-of-function mutations in the CTNS gene, which encodes cystinosin, the lysosomal membrane transporter responsible for exporting cystine. Defective cystine transport leads to intralysosomal cystine accumulation, renal proximal-tubular dysfunction, and the clinical picture of Fanconi syndrome.

831921.long_answer: ABCB6 encodes an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter protein. Pathogenic variants in ABCB6 have been shown to cause dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria (DUH), a genetic disorder characterized by mottled hypo- and hyperpigmented macules on the skin. Thus, mutations in the ABC transporter gene ABCB6 are directly linked to a pigmentation disorder.

356137.long_answer: Dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria (DUH) is caused by mutations in the ATP-binding cassette transporter gene ABCB6. The human ABCB6 gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 2, cytogenetic band q36, establishing chromosome 2q36 as the locus implicated in DUH.

783701.long_answer: In patients with Cushing’s disease, excess cortisol is driven by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma. When both adrenal glands are surgically removed (bilateral adrenalectomy) to eliminate cortisol production, the negative-feedback signal on the pituitary disappears. The pituitary adenoma (or corticotroph cells) often responds by markedly increasing ACTH secretion. This post-adrenalectomy surge of ACTH is a well-recognized biological response and can stimulate further growth of the pituitary tumor. The clinical constellation of rapid pituitary tumor enlargement, very high ACTH levels, skin hyperpigmentation and visual/neurologic symptoms that may follow adrenalectomy is termed Nelson’s syndrome. Thus, persistent or accelerated ACTH secretion after adrenal removal is the key pathophysiologic mechanism underlying the complication, confirming the statement.

550597.long_answer: Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in the CTSC gene, which encodes cathepsin C (also known as dipeptidyl peptidase I), a lysosomal cysteine protease. Cathepsin C deficiency impairs activation of neutrophil serine proteases, leading to severe periodontal destruction and the characteristic palmoplantar keratoderma.

205706.long_answer: Acute (including neonatal) respiratory distress syndrome is frequently linked to deficiency of pulmonary surfactant protein-B. The surfactant protein-B gene (SFTPB), which encodes this critical lung surfactant component, is mapped to chromosome 2 (region 2p11-p12). Mutations or lack of expression of SFTPB on chromosome 2 result in surfactant protein-B deficiency and the consequent development of severe respiratory distress.

131544.long_answer: Paramyotonia congenita is caused by mutations in the SCN4A gene, which encodes the NaV1.4 voltage-gated sodium-channel α-subunit. SCN4A mRNA and its protein product are almost exclusively expressed in adult skeletal (striated) muscle fibers, where they govern action-potential generation and muscle excitability.

329737.long_answer: Paramyotonia congenita results from missense mutations in SCN4A, the gene encoding the NaV1.4 α-subunit of the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated sodium channel. These mutations impair channel fast inactivation, producing persistent sodium influx and the paradoxical myotonia characteristic of this autosomal-dominant disorder.

199779.long_answer: Abderhalden’s original description concerned cystinosis, an autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder. Cystinosis results from loss-of-function mutations in the CTNS gene, which encodes the lysosomal cystine transporter cystinosin. The CTNS gene is situated at 17p13 on chromosome 17, making chromosome 17 the one affected by these pathogenic mutations.

556592.long_answer: Primary hyperparathyroidism characteristically produces sustained hypercalcaemia.  Hypercalcaemia is a recognised, albeit uncommon, precipitant of acute pancreatitis.  Experimental work shows that excess intracellular calcium in pancreatic acinar cells can promote the premature conversion of trypsinogen to trypsin, initiating autodigestion and inflammation of the gland.  Clinical case series and reviews document episodes of acute pancreatitis that resolve after parathyroidectomy or correction of the hypercalcaemia, supporting a causal link.  Thus, saying that primary hyperparathyroidism leads to elevated calcium levels which can activate trypsinogen in the pancreas and cause pancreatitis is consistent with established pathophysiology and clinical evidence; it is not false.

248646.long_answer: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (APS-1), also called APECED, is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AIRE gene. The AIRE gene is located on chromosome 21 at band 21q22.3; hence, the pathogenic mutations responsible for APS-1 reside on chromosome 21.

383702.long_answer: Yes, the statement is false. Sclerosteosis (classically called sclerosteosis 1) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SOST gene, which encodes the secreted glycoprotein sclerostin. Sclerostin belongs to the DAN family of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) antagonists and suppresses Wnt/β-catenin signalling in bone. It is not a member of, nor does it directly regulate the abundance of, ligands or receptors in the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) superfamily. The pathogenesis of sclerosteosis is therefore unrelated to TNF-superfamily proteins; the disease results from absent or markedly reduced sclerostin and consequent excessive bone formation. Hence the claim that SOST mutations cause sclerosteosis by affecting the level of a TNF-superfamily member is not supported by established biomedical knowledge.

677433.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the SOST gene cause the autosomal-recessive high-bone-mass disorders sclerosteosis and van Buchem disease, in which generalized bone overgrowth is seen. SOST encodes sclerostin, an osteocyte-derived glycoprotein that antagonises canonical Wnt/β-catenin signalling in osteoblasts. By dampening Wnt activity, sclerostin reduces osteoprotegerin (OPG) expression; OPG is a decoy receptor that binds RANKL (tumour-necrosis-factor-ligand superfamily member 11) and prevents it from activating its receptor RANK on osteoclast precursors. Thus, normal sclerostin function indirectly restrains (inhibits) RANKL signalling. When SOST is mutated and sclerostin is absent, this brake is lost, OPG levels rise, RANKL activity is suppressed, osteoclastogenesis falls and excessive bone accumulates, producing the characteristic bone overgrowth phenotype.

236323.long_answer: Adenosine monophosphate deaminase (myoadenylate deaminase) deficiency type 1 is caused by mutations in the AMPD1 gene. The AMPD1 gene is mapped to chromosome 1 (band 1p13.2); therefore, the pathogenic mutations responsible for this metabolic myopathy reside on chromosome 1.

901549.long_answer: Several developmental disorders that present with digit malformations, characteristic craniofacial features, intellectual disability and pre-/post-natal growth retardation (e.g., Cornelia de Lange syndrome, Roberts syndrome, mosaic variegated aneuploidy) are caused by loss-of-function mutations in genes such as NIPBL, SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21, ESCO2 or BUB1B. All of these genes encode either core components of the cohesin complex or proteins that regulate the spindle-assembly checkpoint. Cohesin establishment and spindle-checkpoint control are essential for the accurate segregation of sister chromatids during mitosis – the process that yields two genetically identical daughter cells. When these genes are mutated, sister-chromatid cohesion is defective or the mitotic checkpoint fails, leading to chromosome mis-segregation and the clinical phenotype described. Hence, the gene(s) responsible for the disease do indeed affect mitosis, the mechanism that normally produces genetically identical daughter cells.

413785.long_answer: Filippi syndrome is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the CKAP2L gene. CKAP2L encodes a spindle-associated cytoskeletal protein that is critical for assembling the mitotic spindle and properly separating sister chromatids during cell division. The CKAP2L locus is situated on chromosome 2 (band q14), so the disease-causing gene resides on chromosome 2.

985510.long_answer: In DOOR syndrome (Deafness, Onychodystrophy, Osteodystrophy, Intellectual disability), the osteodystrophy refers to malformed distal phalanges of the fingers and toes—the long bones at the tips of the hands and feet that are radiologically broad, hypoplastic, or absent.

787890.long_answer: Mutations in PTPN11, which encodes the SHP-2 protein tyrosine phosphatase, cause Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines (formerly LEOPARD syndrome). A cardinal feature of this disorder is the development of numerous dark brown lentigines (spots) on the skin, directly linking the PTP family member PTPN11 to the pigmentation phenotype.

937806.long_answer: The gene most commonly mutated in Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines is PTPN11, which encodes the SHP-2 tyrosine phosphatase. Somatic activating mutations of PTPN11 are found in roughly one-third of cases of juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML), linking this specific leukemia subtype to the same pathway affected in the syndrome.

940390.long_answer: Anemia is a hematologic disorder marked by an abnormally low red-blood-cell mass or hemoglobin level, reducing the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity. In the fetus, significant anemia forces the heart to pump much harder to maintain oxygen delivery, creating a high-output cardiac state. This cardiac overload can progress to heart failure, leading to widespread fluid accumulation—hydrops fetalis—defined by effusions or edema in at least two fetal compartments.

584175.long_answer: The ADAMTSL4 gene, located at 1q21 on human chromosome 1 (the largest chromosome), is well-established as the cause of autosomal-recessive isolated ectopia lentis. Pathogenic variants in ADAMTSL4 disrupt the extracellular matrix proteins that stabilize the zonular fibers, leading to displacement (subluxation or complete dislocation) of the crystalline lens in the eye.

458328.long_answer: Autosomal recessive isolated ectopia lentis is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ADAMTSL4 gene. ADAMTSL4 is mapped to cytogenetic band 1q21.2 on chromosome 1, establishing chromosome 1 as the chromosomal location associated with this condition.

692671.long_answer: Familial (inherited) primary aldosteronism type III is caused by germ-line mutations in the KCNJ5 gene. KCNJ5 encodes GIRK4, an inward-rectifier potassium channel that is predominantly expressed in the adrenal zona glomerulosa and the pituitary gland. Pathogenic KCNJ5 mutations alter the channel’s selectivity, leading to membrane depolarization, increased calcium influx, and excessive aldosterone production, thereby linking this potassium channel gene to inherited primary aldosteronism.

672286.long_answer: Mutations in the visual-system homeobox gene VSX2 (also called CHX10), which maps to 14q24 on chromosome 14, are responsible for a spectrum of ocular anomalies that include anophthalmia, microphthalmia and severe myopia. Therefore, the gene associated with these three conditions is located on chromosome 14.

297133.long_answer:
Isolated congenital adermatoglyphia is a very mild genetic condition: the primary finding is absence or marked reduction of fingerprint ridges. Reported accompanying features are minor (e.g., slightly decreased palmar sweating, occasional acral blistering) and there is no systemic organ involvement or reduction in life expectancy. 

By contrast, the disorder historically referred to as Baird syndrome (now more commonly called Bardet–Biedl syndrome) is a multisystem ciliopathy. It typically includes progressive retinal dystrophy leading to blindness, renal malformations and renal failure, obesity, polydactyly, hypogonadism, metabolic disturbances and cognitive/behavioral problems, together with their numerous secondary complications. 

Because Bardet–Biedl/Baird syndrome affects several organ systems and is associated with substantial morbidity, whereas adermatoglyphia is limited almost entirely to the skin ridges with only very minor additional manifestations, adermatoglyphia clearly has far fewer ‘side effects’ or clinical complications. Consequently, the statement in the question is consistent with established medical knowledge.

896881.long_answer: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) is encoded by the AVP gene on chromosome 20p13. When AVP production or action is impaired, urine cannot be concentrated properly at night, leading to excessive nocturnal urine output and thus enuresis (bed-wetting).

889269.long_answer: Glycine encephalopathy (non-ketotic hyperglycinemia) is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in genes encoding the glycine-cleavage system (e.g., GLDC, AMT, GCSH). It follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern and is considered an ultra-rare inborn error of metabolism. Propionic acidemia results from biallelic variants in PCCA or PCCB that impair propionyl-CoA carboxylase activity. This condition is likewise inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and is classified as a rare organic acidemia. Therefore, both disorders are indeed rare metabolic conditions transmitted by autosomal recessive inheritance.

286064.long_answer: Cystinuria is an inherited renal tubular disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the SLC3A1 and SLC7A9 genes, which encode the two subunits of the cystine-dibasic amino acid transporter in the proximal tubule. Loss of transporter function prevents re-absorption of cystine, lysine, arginine and ornithine, so large amounts of poorly soluble cystine accumulate in the urine and precipitate as cystine kidney stones.

478250.long_answer: A study in Egyptian infants demonstrated that susceptibility to biliary atresia is linked to a promoter polymorphism in the interleukin-18 (IL-18) gene. The human IL-18 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 11q22–q23 on chromosome 11, making chromosome 11 the chromosomal location of the gene implicated in these Egyptian cases of biliary atresia.

864810.long_answer: Carpenter syndrome with brachydactyly is most commonly caused by pathogenic variants in the RAB23 gene. RAB23 is mapped to the short arm of chromosome 6 (region 6p11–p12), so the causal gene for Carpenter syndrome is located on chromosome 6.

332073.long_answer: Mucopolysaccharidoses result from dysfunction of lysosomes. The lysosome was discovered by Christian de Duve, who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1974 (shared with Albert Claude and George E. Palade) for elucidating the structural and functional organization of the cell, including lysosomal biology.

412837.long_answer: Congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ib (CDG-Ib) results from deficiency of phosphomannose isomerase, the enzyme that reversibly converts fructose-6-phosphate to mannose-6-phosphate. Loss of this step limits mannose-1-phosphate and GDP-mannose production, impairing N-linked glycan assembly and producing the characteristic CDG-Ib clinical and biochemical phenotype.

717741.long_answer: The HFE gene that causes hereditary haemochromatosis type 1 is located on the short arm of chromosome 6 (region 6p21.3-p22), where it encodes an MHC class-I–like protein involved in iron homeostasis.

495147.long_answer: Lymphedema–distichiasis syndrome is most commonly caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the FOXC2 gene. FOXC2 is a member of the forkhead box (FOX) family of transcription factors, so the first part of the statement is correct. However, the canonical human FOXC2 protein (UniProt Q99958; RefSeq NP_005242.3) is 501 amino acids long, not 504 amino acids. Although alternative splice variants with different lengths have been reported, a 504-residue form is not the accepted reference length used in the medical-genetics literature. Therefore the complete statement as worded is not accurate.

487758.long_answer: The LIS1 gene (also known as PAFAH1B1), whose haploinsufficiency causes the classical autosomal form of lissencephaly, is mapped to the short arm of chromosome 17 at band 17p13.3.

564328.long_answer: Parkinson’s disease is defined by the cardinal motor signs of parkinsonism—resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, and postural instability. Dementia with Lewy bodies belongs to the same Lewy-body disease spectrum; its clinical diagnostic criteria list "parkinsonism" (defined as bradykinesia plus at least one of rest tremor or rigidity) as a core feature, and patients typically manifest bradykinesia, rigidity, postural instability and, in many cases, tremor (although the tremor is often less prominent than in idiopathic Parkinson’s disease). Therefore these four motor symptoms are considered characteristic and commonly encountered in both Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson’s disease.

939230.long_answer: Nijmegen breakage syndrome is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the NBN gene (also called NBS1 or nibrin). The NBN gene is located on chromosome 8 at band 8q21.3. Chromosome 8 contains about 145–146 million base pairs. Given that the entire diploid human genome is ~3.2 billion base pairs, chromosome 8 represents approximately 4.5 % of the total nuclear DNA (146 Mb ÷ 3,200 Mb ≈ 0.0456). This proportion falls within the 4.5–5 % range stated in the question. Therefore, the statement is consistent with established genomic data.

293751.long_answer: KRT6A, the keratin-6A gene on chromosome 12q13, is one of the principal genes mutated in pachyonychia congenita. Pathogenic variants disturb the keratin filament network in stratified epithelia, producing nail dystrophy, palmoplantar keratoderma and characteristic thick white patches (oral leukokeratosis) on the oral mucosa. These leukokeratotic lesions are recognised as a form of oral leukoplakia, a premalignant condition that carries an increased risk for progression to oral squamous cell carcinoma, establishing KRT6A as the gene linking both pachyonychia congenita and cancer-prone oral white patches.

146675.long_answer: Lactate dehydrogenase-A (LDH-A) deficiency is produced by pathogenic variants in the LDHA gene, which encodes the A (muscle/erythrocyte) subunit of lactate dehydrogenase. Glycogen-storage disease type XI (Fanconi-Bickel syndrome) is caused by mutations in the SLC2A2 gene that encodes the facilitative glucose transporter GLUT2. These are two completely different genes located on different chromosomes and involved in distinct metabolic pathways. Therefore LDH-A deficiency is not caused by the same gene that is mutated in GSD XI.

485841.long_answer: The SQSTM1 gene encodes sequestosome-1 (p62), a ubiquitin-binding cargo adaptor that links poly-ubiquitinated proteins to LC3 on the autophagosome membrane, thereby directing them for selective autophagy. Germ-line mutations in SQSTM1 are a well-established cause of Paget's disease of bone, making it the gene requested.

728328.long_answer: In the hepatic urea cycle, the first and rate-limiting mitochondrial enzyme is carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase I (CPS I). CPS I is allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate. When CPS I itself is deficient, or when N-acetylglutamate synthase is deficient (preventing formation of the activator), the urea cycle cannot effectively convert toxic ammonia to urea, leading to hyperammonemia. Thus, there is indeed a mitochondrial, N-acetylglutamate-regulated enzyme whose deficiency causes the accumulation of ammonia in the blood.

289441.long_answer: Plasmodium falciparum is an apicomplexan (alveolate) protozoan parasite transmitted solely by bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. It causes the most severe form of malaria, whose clinical spectrum spans periodic fever, chills, and fatigue to life-threatening complications such as cerebral malaria, coma, and death.

513990.long_answer:
The gene that encodes connexin-31 is GJB3.  Different pathogenic variants in GJB3 have been documented in two quite distinct clinical settings:
•  Erythrokeratodermia variabilis (EKV): several missense mutations (e.g., p.Gly12Asp, p.Asp50Asn) produce the typical migratory erythema and hyperkeratosis of EKV.
•  Non-syndromic sensorineural hearing loss: other GJB3 mutations (e.g., p.Val37Ile, p.Phe52Leu, p.Trp77Ser, p.Asp166His) have been found in families and sporadic cases with autosomal-dominant or autosomal-recessive deafness in the absence of skin disease.  These variants disrupt gap-junction communication in cochlear supporting cells but may leave epidermal function largely intact.

Thus, mutations in the connexin-31 gene that is classically linked to EKV can indeed present solely with non-syndromic deafness, depending on the specific allele and its functional effect.  This is well-accepted in the otogenetic and dermatologic literature, so the statement is supported by established biomedical consensus.

828299.long_answer: The NF2 gene, whose mutations are found in roughly 25 % of sporadic meningiomas, gives rise to many splice transcripts, but only two distinct Merlin protein isoforms (≈595-aa and 590-aa) have been demonstrated and characterized in mammalian cells.

831229.long_answer: Carey-Fineman-Ziter syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the MYMK (myomaker) gene. MYMK is an essential fusogenic membrane protein that enables mononucleated myoblasts to merge. When MYMK is mutated, myoblasts remain separate and cannot fuse, so the normal multinucleated myotubes (developing skeletal muscle fibers) fail to form, leading to the muscle weakness and craniofacial anomalies characteristic of the syndrome.

123584.long_answer: Isolated hereditary hypermethioninemia is most commonly produced by pathogenic variants in genes that participate directly in methionine metabolism, especially MAT1A (methionine-adenosyltransferase I/III), and more rarely GNMT or AHCY. By contrast, the three classical forms of hereditary tyrosinemia are caused by defects in enzymes of the tyrosine-catabolic pathway: FAH for tyrosinemia type I, TAT for type II, and HPD for type III. None of these tyrosinemia genes are the same as the genes responsible for primary hypermethioninemia. Although patients with tyrosinemia type I often develop secondary hypermethioninemia because of liver dysfunction, the underlying genetic mutations are different. Therefore, hypermethioninemia and tyrosinemia are not caused by mutations in the same genes.

694090.long_answer: Several transcription factors are critical for maintaining self-renewal and pluripotency of embryonic stem (ES) cells, the most prominent being SOX2, POU5F1/OCT4, and NANOG. Among these, heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in SOX2 are a well-established cause of severe ocular malformations, most notably anophthalmia and microphthalmia (termed SOX2-anophthalmia syndrome). SOX2 encodes an HMG-box transcription factor required both for ES-cell pluripotency and for early eye field specification during embryogenesis. Human genetic studies and animal models show that SOX2 haploinsufficiency disrupts optic cup formation, leading to markedly reduced eye size (microphthalmia) or absence of the eye (anophthalmia). Therefore, a mutation in a gene encoding a transcription factor essential for ES-cell self-renewal and pluripotency can indeed result in microphthalmia, with SOX2 providing a clear, consensus-supported example.

660612.long_answer: In humans the BMP4 (Bone Morphogenetic Protein 4) gene maps to cytogenetic band 14q22-q23 on chromosome 14. Mutations or dosage alterations at this locus have been associated with ocular malformations such as anophthalmia, and BMP4 signalling intersects functionally with the Sonic hedgehog (SHH) developmental pathway.

462009.long_answer: Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is an extremely rare congenital malformation syndrome first described by Berk and Tabatznik. In the handful of patients that have been documented, radiographic examination revealed generalized shortening of the phalanges – particularly the distal phalanges – of both the fingers and the toes. This skeletal feature is termed brachyphalangy or brachydactyly, i.e., a condition in which one or more phalanges are smaller/shorter than normal. The presence of brachyphalangy is repeatedly cited as one of the cardinal findings in the original case reports as well as in subsequent summaries in the medical genetics literature (e.g., OMIM and Orphanet entries). Therefore, the syndrome is indeed associated with a condition in which one or more of the phalanges of the digits are smaller than normal.

975569.long_answer: Scopophobia (also called scoptophobia or ophthalmophobia) is the persistent, irrational fear of being looked at, watched, or stared at by other people. The fear of erubescence (blushing) is a different specific phobia, most commonly termed erythrophobia or erubescophobia. Although someone who fears being stared at might also dread blushing in public, the two conditions are classified separately in the clinical and psychiatric literature. Therefore, scopophobia is not the same as the fear of erubescence.

969689.long_answer:
Although both Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD) and Cystic Fibrosis (CF) are inherited diseases that lead to defective mucociliary clearance and chronic airway infection, they arise from mutations in completely different genes. 

• Cystic Fibrosis is caused by pathogenic variants in a single gene, CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator), located on chromosome 7. Defects in CFTR impair chloride and bicarbonate transport across epithelial cells, thickening mucus throughout multiple organs.

• Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia is genetically heterogeneous: more than 50 different genes have been implicated (e.g., DNAH5, DNAH11, DNAI1, CCDC39, CCDC40, RSPH4A). These genes encode structural or regulatory components of motile cilia; their dysfunction leads to impaired ciliary beat, not to CFTR channel dysfunction.

Because the molecular bases of the two diseases involve non-overlapping gene sets (CFTR for CF vs. ciliary structural/assembly genes for PCD), the statement that they are associated with the same set of genes is incorrect.

123467.long_answer: Maffucci syndrome is now known to be caused by somatic (mosaic) activating mutations in the isocitrate dehydrogenase genes IDH1 and IDH2. IDH1 is located on chromosome 2q33.3, whereas IDH2 is located on chromosome 15q26.1. No commonly accepted disease-causing gene for Maffucci syndrome resides on chromosome 14. Therefore, saying that the two genes most commonly associated with the syndrome are on chromosomes 2 and 14 is not consistent with established genomic data.

506648.long_answer:
Maternal pre-gestational (overt) diabetes is indeed a recognized prenatal teratogen for a broad group of congenital heart defects, but the strength of the association is not the same for all lesions. Large population-based studies and meta-analyses consistently show one of the highest relative risks for conotruncal malformations such as transposition of the great arteries (TGA), with odds ratios generally in the 3- to 5-fold (and sometimes higher) range compared with non-diabetic pregnancies.  

For Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) the association with maternal diabetes is weaker and often of borderline statistical significance; reported odds ratios are usually lower (≈1.5–3) and some studies do not find a significant excess at all once other factors are controlled.  

Because of this difference, current teratology reviews, epidemiologic surveys (e.g., Botto et al., 2001; Lisowski et al., 2010; EUROCAT data), and textbook summaries list maternal diabetes as a strong risk factor for TGA, whereas for TOF it is described as a possible or moderate risk factor. They are therefore not regarded as risk factors of "equal magnitude" for the two defects.  

Consequently, the statement that maternal diabetes mellitus is considered a prenatal risk factor of equal magnitude in both transposition of the great vessels and Tetralogy of Fallot is not supported by the established scientific consensus.

226088.long_answer: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a quintessential pro-inflammatory cytokine whose circulating and gingival levels rise markedly in periodontal disease. The IL6 gene resides on chromosome 7p15-p21 and consists of five exons, matching the genomic description provided.

213664.long_answer:
Both disorders are classified as forms of (congenital or acquired) pure red-cell aplasia. 
• Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) – whether acquired, drug-induced, autoimmune or parvovirus-related – is defined by severe anemia with virtual absence of erythroid precursors in the marrow. Granulopoiesis and megakaryopoiesis remain intact, so white-blood-cell and platelet counts are typically normal.
• Diamond–Blackfan anemia (DBA) is a congenital/pediatric form of pure red-cell aplasia caused by ribosomal-protein gene mutations. It produces macrocytic anemia and reticulocytopenia, again with preserved myeloid and megakaryocytic lineages. Although mild neutropenia can occasionally be seen, the white-blood-cell count is generally within normal limits and not the main cytopenia.
Therefore, the common feature of both PRCA and DBA is isolated red-cell deficiency; the white blood cells are not significantly affected in most cases, making the statement correct.

343459.long_answer:
Both clonal hypereosinophilia (e.g., chronic eosinophilic leukaemia, myeloid neoplasms with FIP1L1-PDGFRA or PDGFRB rearrangements) and common allergic/atopic diseases such as asthma, rhinitis or eczema are characterized by elevated peripheral-blood and tissue eosinophil counts. However, the biological drivers are different.

• Clonal (primary) hypereosinophilia: The eosinophils arise from an abnormal haematopoietic clone that carries oncogenic mutations or chromosomal rearrangements. Proliferation is autonomous, cytokine-independent and persists even in the absence of external stimuli. WHO classifications place these disorders among myeloproliferative neoplasms.

• Reactive (secondary) eosinophilia in allergy/asthma: Eosinophil expansion is polyclonal and driven by immune activation. Allergen exposure triggers Th2 lymphocytes to secrete IL-5, IL-4, IL-13 and eotaxins, which promote eosinophil differentiation in the bone marrow and recruitment to tissues. Removal of the allergen or control of inflammation typically normalises eosinophil counts.

Thus, while both settings feature increased eosinophil numbers, clonal hypereosinophilia results from an intrinsic malignant clone whereas allergy/asthma involve cytokine-mediated, reversible, reactive eosinophilia. This distinction is well established in haematology and allergy/immunology consensus guidelines.

360820.long_answer: DC-SIGN (Dendritic Cell-Specific ICAM-3-Grabbing Non-integrin) is encoded in humans by the CD209 gene. CD209 produces a C-type lectin receptor expressed on dendritic cells that recognizes high-mannose glycans on pathogens such as the West Nile virus, promoting viral attachment and entry into host cells.

700500.long_answer: Norman-Roberts syndrome is an autosomal-recessive form of lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia that results from loss-of-function mutations in the RELN gene. RELN encodes the extracellular matrix glycoprotein reelin, a key regulator of neuronal migration and cortical lamination. Absence of functional reelin disrupts normal brain layering, producing the smooth cortex and cerebellar underdevelopment seen in Norman-Roberts syndrome.

834335.long_answer: Sialidosis is caused by a deficiency of lysosomal neuraminidase (sialidase), which is encoded by the NEU1 gene on chromosome 6p21.3. Fucosidosis results from a deficiency of lysosomal α-L-fucosidase, encoded by the FUCA1 gene on chromosome 1p36–p34. Because the responsible genes are located on different chromosomes (chromosome 6 vs. chromosome 1), the deficient enzymes in sialidosis and fucosidosis are not encoded on the same chromosome.

212762.long_answer: Fanconi anemia proteins form the FA pathway, which cooperates with BRCA1/BRCA2 and other factors to repair DNA interstrand cross-links by homologous recombination—a repair mechanism that exchanges genetic information between identical or highly similar DNA sequences to restore accurate DNA structure.

381141.long_answer: Xanthinuria results from deficiency of the enzyme xanthine oxidase ⁄ xanthine dehydrogenase. The catalytic center of this enzyme contains a molybdenum-pterin cofactor; the molybdenum ion is essential for the oxidation of xanthine and hypoxanthine to uric acid. Hence, molybdenum is the metal present in the enzyme’s active site.

150566.long_answer: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) results from reactivation of JC virus, a human polyomavirus. In immunocompromised individuals the virus infects and lyses oligodendrocytes, the myelinating cells of the central nervous system, leading to widespread demyelination and the characteristic multifocal white-matter lesions of the disease.

728848.long_answer: The form of hereditary hemochromatosis most frequent in people of Celtic ancestry is linked to mutations (especially C282Y) in the HFE gene, which is located on the short arm of chromosome 6 at band 6p21.3 near the HLA region.

224272.long_answer: Pemphigus foliaceus is characterized by IgG autoantibodies that bind desmoglein-1, a desmosomal adhesion protein. The exfoliative (ETA/ETB) toxins of Staphylococcus aureus that produce staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome specifically cleave the same protein, desmoglein-1. Desmoglein-1 is encoded by the DSG1 gene; therefore, DSG1 is the gene common to both conditions.

200636.long_answer: The desmoglein-1 gene (DSG1), which encodes the desmosomal cadherin desmoglein-1, is part of the desmosomal cadherin gene cluster mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 18 (region 18q12).

719196.long_answer: Rubella virus is spread person-to-person through respiratory droplets. Individuals with rubella are considered infectious from roughly 7 days before the rash appears until about 7 days after the rash onset. The 'third day of rubella symptoms' therefore falls well within this contagious window. A person who is not immune—because they are unvaccinated or have never had rubella—can readily become infected after close contact during this period. Consequently, the non-immune individual in the conversation is at genuine risk of contracting rubella.

798687.long_answer: Recessive mutations in the CAPN3 gene (calpain-3) are the leading cause of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy in many Eurasian populations (classified as LGMD2A/R1). In northern European populations, the most common form of the same condition is produced by mutations in the FKRP gene, giving rise to LGMD2I/R9. Thus, the muscular disease primarily linked to both CAPN3 and FKRP defects is limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.

435050.long_answer: The SLC2A9 gene encodes the facilitative transporter GLUT9.  GLUT9 is a high-capacity urate transporter that mediates reabsorption and export of uric acid, and genetic variants in SLC2A9 are a well-established cause of familial hyperuricemia and gout.  Beyond its renal role, GLUT9 is expressed in cartilage where it contributes to nutrient/urate handling required for growth-plate maturation; loss-of-function studies show that it influences differentiation and development of chondrocytes.  Thus SLC2A9 links uric-acid transport with chondrocyte development and the clinical phenotypes of hyperuricemia and gout.

891164.long_answer: Homozygous mutations in the TRAPPC11 gene cause limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2S (LGMD R18). In patient cells the glycosylation defect can be partially corrected by supplying mevalonate/mevalonolactone, suggesting potential therapeutic benefit. The TRAPPC11 gene is situated on chromosome 4, so chromosome 4 is the chromosome that harbours the gene whose homozygous mutation produces this mevalonolactone-responsive form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.

960406.long_answer: Friedreich's ataxia is caused by markedly reduced levels of the protein frataxin. Frataxin is localized to the mitochondrial matrix, where it participates in iron–sulfur cluster assembly and regulation of mitochondrial iron homeostasis. Thus, the organelle that contains the deficient protein in Friedreich's ataxia is the mitochondrion.

589778.long_answer: McArdle’s disease (glycogen-storage disease type V) results from mutations in the PYGM gene encoding muscle glycogen phosphorylase. These mutations abolish the enzyme’s glycogen phosphorylase activity, preventing normal glycogenolysis in skeletal muscle and leading to the characteristic exercise intolerance and muscle cramps.

692493.long_answer: Familial pulmonary veno-occlusive disease is caused by biallelic mutations in the EIF2AK4 gene (encoding GCN2). The EIF2AK4 locus is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 15 (15q15), so the gene responsible for PVOD resides on chromosome 15.

284967.long_answer: Parastremmatic dwarfism is a severe skeletal dysplasia in which abnormal bone formation and deformity can cause pathological fusion of joint structures. This fusion, called ankylosis, results in stiffness and loss of range of motion, thereby limiting normal joint movement.

347813.long_answer: Chickenpox is an acute viral exanthem caused by the varicella-zoster virus (a human herpesvirus). Pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta (PLEVA) can clinically resemble chickenpox because both conditions produce crops of vesicopustular lesions that crust over. However, extensive virologic, histopathologic and epidemiologic studies show that PLEVA is not caused by varicella-zoster virus or by any other known herpesvirus. PLEVA is classified as an inflammatory/lymphoproliferative skin disorder of uncertain etiology; proposed triggers include dysregulated T-cell immune responses and, in some cases, preceding infections such as streptococcal or viral illnesses, but not VZV. Polymerase-chain-reaction testing of PLEVA lesions is consistently negative for VZV DNA, further confirming the absence of the chickenpox virus. Therefore, while PLEVA may be mistaken for chickenpox on clinical grounds, it is not caused by the same virus.

655179.long_answer: The FKH-14 gene (now named FOXC2) encodes a forkhead family transcription factor. Pathogenic FOXC2 mutations produce lymphedema-distichiasis syndrome, whose hallmark is distichiasis—development of a second row of eyelashes originating from the Meibomian glands.

786981.long_answer: The form of epidermolytic hyperkeratosis that includes palm-plantar involvement is produced by pathogenic variants in the keratin-1 (KRT1) gene, which is located on chromosome 12q13. In contrast, mutations in keratin-10 on chromosome 17 typically spare the palms and soles. Thus, chromosome 12 is the chromosome implicated in the palmoplantar-involving variant.

153852.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1. The FBN1 gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 15 (15q21.1), making chromosome 15 the locus of the genetic defect responsible for this hereditary connective tissue disorder.

120745.long_answer: The majority of autosomal dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia (classified as SPG4) is caused by mutations in the SPAST gene on chromosome 2p22, which encodes the microtubule-severing ATPase spastin. Loss-of-function variants in SPAST disrupt axonal microtubule dynamics, leading to corticospinal tract degeneration and the characteristic progressive spasticity, making it the most common genetic cause of autosomal dominant spastic paraplegia.

601233.long_answer: Both fissured tongue and geographic tongue (also called benign migratory glossitis) are classed as benign oral mucosal conditions.
