They are developmental or idiopathic variations of normal anatomy, are not premalignant, and in the vast majority of cases require no treatment other than reassurance and, occasionally, symptomatic management (e.g., addressing irritation or secondary infection). Therefore, the statement that both are benign conditions is supported by established clinical consensus.

755725.long_answer: Although the etiology of Gómez-López-Hernández syndrome is still uncertain, several patients with the condition (or with the key malformation rhombencephalosynapsis that defines it) have been found to carry pathogenic variants in the MAST1 gene, which is located on chromosome 19q13. This implicates alterations on chromosome 19 as a possible molecular contributor to the syndrome.

110703.long_answer: Glycogen storage disease type II (Pompe disease) is caused by mutations in the GAA gene on chromosome 17; this gene is autosomal and the disorder is inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner. In contrast, Danon disease results from mutations in the LAMP2 gene located on the X chromosome (Xq24), and the condition shows X-linked dominant inheritance. Because only one of the two diseases involves an autosomal gene, the statement that the genes mutated in both disorders are autosomal is incorrect.

465164.long_answer:
Wolf–Hirschhorn syndrome (WHS) is the prototypical microdeletion/contiguous-gene syndrome caused by a small (usually 3–5 Mb or smaller) sub-microscopic deletion at 4p16.3; it is therefore universally listed among the classical microdeletion syndromes.  

Ring chromosome 18, in contrast, is defined by breakpoints at both ends of chromosome 18 with circularization of the chromosome and loss of the terminal segments. The resulting deleted segments are generally large enough to be visible on routine karyotyping, and the abnormality is classified as a “ring chromosome disorder,” not as a microdeletion syndrome. Although individuals with ring 18 may lose distal 18p and 18q material, the mechanism (ring formation with variable, often macroscopically detectable loss and mosaicism) and the clinical category are different from the group of well-defined microdeletion syndromes detected only by FISH/CMA.  

Therefore, while Wolf–Hirschhorn syndrome is a microdeletion syndrome, ring chromosome 18 is not, so the statement that both are microdeletion syndromes is incorrect.

792492.long_answer: Both the World Health Organization (WHO) and other consensus panels define hypereosinophilia for hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) and for chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL, NOS) as an absolute peripheral-blood eosinophil count of ≥1.5 × 10^9/L (≥1500 cells/µL). Whereas additional requirements differ (HES needs persistence and organ involvement; CEL needs evidence of a clonal myeloid neoplasm or increased blasts), the purely numeric eosinophil-count criterion is the same in both disorders. Therefore, with respect to eosinophil counts, the diagnostic criteria are identical.

689083.long_answer: Vibrio cholerae—the bacterium Pouchet reported in 1849 as a protozoan—produces cholera toxin. That toxin binds specifically to the GM1 ganglioside, a glycosphingolipid on intestinal epithelial cells. In the rare hereditary sphingolipidosis called GM1 gangliosidosis, congenital deficiency of lysosomal β-galactosidase causes massive intracellular accumulation of the same GM1 ganglioside. Thus GM1 gangliosidosis is the disorder characterized by build-up of the compound that serves as the cholera toxin receptor.

341684.long_answer:
Generalized arterial calcification of infancy (GACI) is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused most often by pathogenic variants in ENPP1 or ABCC6. Because the gene defect is not sex-linked, published case series and registry data show an approximately 1:1 male-to-female ratio; therefore the disease is considered to affect males and females equally.

Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL), in contrast, shows a clear sex predilection. Large epidemiologic studies from Japan, Korea, and North America consistently report a higher prevalence in men, with male-to-female ratios ranging from about 1.5:1 to 2.5:1 for cervical OPLL (the most common form). While thoracic OPLL may occur relatively more often in women, the overall condition is still significantly more frequent in males.

Because OPLL does not affect males and females equally, the statement that both GACI and OPLL affect males and females equally is incorrect.

758030.long_answer: Freiberg’s disease (also called Freiberg infraction) is an osteochondrosis/avascular necrosis that primarily involves the head of a metatarsal, most often the second metatarsal in the forefoot. Preiser’s disease, in contrast, is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the carpal scaphoid bone in the wrist occurring in the absence of a fracture. Thus, the two conditions are both forms of avascular necrosis but they affect entirely different skeletal sites—the metatarsal head in the foot versus the scaphoid in the wrist—making them distinct clinical entities.

941574.long_answer:
Hypertelorism (abnormally increased distance between the orbits) is a reported facial feature in the published descriptions of both disorders:

1. Porencephaly-cerebellar hypoplasia-internal malformations syndrome – The handful of cases described in the literature show a characteristic facial dysmorphism that includes a broad forehead, epicanthic folds and clearly stated hypertelorism, together with CNS lesions (porencephalic cysts, cerebellar hypoplasia) and multiple visceral malformations.

2. Holoprosencephaly-ectrodactyly-cleft lip/palate (Hartsfield/HEC) syndrome – Reviews and case reports of this syndrome list ocular hypertelorism among its recurrent cranio-facial manifestations, along with midline clefts, holoprosencephaly and split-hand/foot malformations.

Because hypertelorism is documented as a component of the dysmorphic facial phenotype in both syndromes, the statement is supported by the established clinical descriptions.

283531.long_answer:
Porencephaly-cerebellar hypoplasia-internal malformations syndrome has only been reported in sibships born to healthy, consanguineous parents; on that basis it is regarded as an autosomal-recessive multiple-congenital-anomalies disorder.

Holoprosencephaly-ectrodactyly-cleft lip/palate syndrome (also known as Hartsfield syndrome or holoprosencephaly-ectrodactyly syndrome) is genetically heterogeneous.  Most molecularly proven cases are caused by de-novo heterozygous or mosaic pathogenic variants in FGFR1 and therefore follow an autosomal-dominant pattern; a few families with biallelic FGFR1 variants showing autosomal-recessive transmission have also been described.  Because the disorder can be (and most often is) autosomal dominant, it is not correct to state that it is strictly autosomal recessive.

Therefore, while the first syndrome is regarded as autosomal recessive, the second is not exclusively so; consequently the statement that both disorders are autosomal-recessive is incorrect.

491834.long_answer:
Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (NAIT) and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) both produce thrombocytopenia, but by very different pathophysiologic routes.

• NAIT: Maternal IgG alloantibodies directed against paternally derived platelet-specific antigens (most often HPA-1a) cross the placenta. These antibodies opsonize the fetus’s/neonate’s platelets, which are then removed by the reticulo-endothelial system (immune-mediated destruction). Coagulation pathways are otherwise normal; the platelet loss is antibody driven.

• DIC: A systemic trigger (e.g., sepsis, hypoxia, placental abruption) causes widespread activation of the coagulation cascade. Large amounts of thrombin generate fibrin microthrombi throughout the vasculature, consuming platelets and clotting factors (consumptive coagulopathy). The fall in platelet count is due to accelerated use, not antibody-mediated destruction.

Because NAIT is an immune-mediated clearance of platelets, whereas DIC is a consumptive coagulopathy secondary to uncontrolled coagulation activation, the underlying mechanisms are fundamentally different. Therefore, the mechanisms causing thrombocytopenia in NAIT and DIC are not the same.

778662.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the ESCO2 gene disrupt sister-chromatid cohesion. They were first identified in classic Roberts syndrome and were subsequently found in families diagnosed with SC (pseudothalidomide) phocomelia syndrome, establishing that ESCO2 mutations underlie both conditions—which are now considered allelic variants of the same rare autosomal-recessive malformation syndrome.

446652.long_answer: The canonical human LHCGR (luteinizing hormone/choriogonadotropin receptor) protein, as documented in reference databases such as UniProt (accession P22888), is 699 amino acids long. In contrast, the canonical human GIPC1 (GAIP-interacting protein, C-terminus 1) protein (UniProt accession Q9NQY0) is 333 amino acids long. Since 699 > 333, LHCGR contains substantially more amino acids than GIPC1. Hence the statement is correct.

332135.long_answer: The disorder is caused by pathogenic variants in the UBA1 gene (ubiquitin-like modifier activating enzyme 1). UBA1 is mapped to cytogenetic band Xp11.23-p11.3 on the X chromosome, so the gene responsible for X-linked spinal muscular atrophy type 2 / arthrogryposis multiplex congenita X-linked type 1 resides on the X chromosome.

116951.long_answer: Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus usually produces herpes zoster (shingles) with a unilateral vesicular rash. When the virus reactivates but the typical cutaneous eruption is absent, the condition is called zoster sine herpete—a rash-less (sine herpete) variant that nevertheless presents with the dermatomal pain and neurologic features of shingles.

740216.long_answer: Succinate dehydrogenase (complex II) is the sole enzyme that participates in both the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Deficiency of this enzyme causes mitochondrial complex II deficiency. Almost all pathogenic variants are autosomal-recessive, but a single heterozygous missense change (p.Arg554Trp) in the SDHA gene has been documented to act in an autosomal-dominant fashion—the only known dominant variant for this disorder. The SDHA gene is located on chromosome 5p15, hence chromosome 5 harbors the gene with the unique dominant pathogenic variant linked to succinate dehydrogenase deficiency.

905206.long_answer: Hemoglobin C is produced when a point mutation (Glu6Lys) occurs in the β-globin gene (HBB). The entire β-globin gene cluster, including HBB, is located on the short arm of chromosome 11 at band p15.5. Therefore, the gene responsible for Hemoglobin C production resides on chromosome 11.

531106.long_answer: The β-globin gene (HBB) that carries the Glu6→Lys point mutation responsible for Hemoglobin C is situated on the short arm of chromosome 11 (11p15.4–p15.5), where all β-like globin genes are clustered.

765640.long_answer: Clinical severity in sex-chromosome aneuploidies rises with each additional X chromosome. Individuals with the 48,XXXY karyotype typically show greater intellectual disability, more pronounced hypogonadism, skeletal anomalies, and a higher frequency of congenital heart and genitourinary defects than classic Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY). Therefore, 48,XXXY syndrome is associated with more severe manifestations and a higher risk of congenital abnormalities.

628353.long_answer: NARP syndrome is caused by pathogenic mutations in the mitochondrial gene MT-ATP6. MT-ATP6 encodes ATP synthase subunit 6 (also called subunit a), an essential component of the Fo sector of mitochondrial ATP synthase responsible for proton translocation during oxidative phosphorylation.

166564.long_answer: Autosomal dominant non-syndromic hearing loss type DFNA36 is caused by pathogenic variants in the TMC1 (transmembrane channel-like 1) gene. Cytogenetic mapping places TMC1 on chromosome 9 at band q21.13 (within the broader q21–q22 interval). Hence, the gene responsible for the 36th described type of autosomal dominant non-syndromic deafness (DFNA36) is indeed located in the 9q21-q22 region.

830268.long_answer: Glycogen storage disease type XI is the muscle isoform of lactate dehydrogenase deficiency, produced by pathogenic variants in the LDHA gene, which encodes the A (muscle) subunit of lactate dehydrogenase. Loss-of-function LDHA mutations impair anaerobic glycolysis, leading to exertional myopathy and hemolytic anemia characteristic of this glycogen storage disorder.

811227.long_answer:
Choroidal neovascularization (CNV) is well known to be driven by over-expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF); elevated intraocular VEGF levels and the clinical efficacy of anti-VEGF agents in CNV are firmly established.  

Serpiginous choroiditis, by contrast, is considered a primary inflammatory/choriocapillaris occlusive disease believed to be autoimmune or infectious in origin. Its routine management relies on corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants, not on anti-VEGF therapy.  Except when secondary CNV develops as a complication, studies have not shown consistently elevated VEGF levels in eyes with serpiginous choroiditis itself, and anti-VEGF agents are not part of standard treatment for the underlying inflammation.  

Therefore, while CNV is clearly associated with elevated VEGF, serpiginous choroiditis is not, so the statement that both conditions are associated with elevated VEGF is not supported by established scientific consensus.

151226.long_answer: In congenital renal dysplasia (e.g., multicystic dysplastic kidney) the affected kidney is poorly formed and contributes little or no functional nephron mass. To maintain overall glomerular filtration rate, the unaffected contralateral kidney typically undergoes compensatory (adaptive) hypertrophy—an increase in size and nephron workload. This macroscopic enlargement is a well-described, expected finding in both pediatric radiology and nephrology literature, reflecting normal physiologic adaptation rather than pathology in the remaining kidney. Hence, the contralateral kidney can and often does become hypertrophic when its partner is dysplastic.

571628.long_answer: Fish-eye disease results from deficiency of the enzyme phosphatidylcholine-sterol O-acyltransferase, encoded by the LCAT gene. Genomic mapping studies have placed the human LCAT gene at cytogenetic band 16q22, confirming that it resides on chromosome 16.

872323.long_answer: Combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria (CMAMMA) is caused by pathogenic variants in the ACSF3 gene. Cytogenetically, ACSF3 is situated on the long arm of chromosome 16 at band q24.3 (16q24.3), which is the accepted chromosomal location associated with this disorder.

833665.long_answer: The protein Thespin (encoded by the TEPSIN/C17orf56 gene) associates stoichiometrically with the four core subunits of the heterotetrameric Adaptor Protein Complex 4. It is therefore considered an accessory component of the AP-4 vesicular-trafficking complex that mediates sorting of membrane cargo at the trans-Golgi network.

478238.long_answer: Proteus syndrome—named after the shapeshifting sea god Proteus—is a rare progressive overgrowth disorder. It is caused by mosaic, activating mutations in the AKT1 gene (most commonly c.49G>A, p.E17K), which dysregulate the PI3K–AKT signaling pathway and drive the asymmetric tissue overgrowth characteristic of the syndrome.

849453.long_answer: Cystinuria is caused by pathogenic variants in two transport-related genes: SLC3A1 and SLC7A9. SLC7A9 encodes the b0,+AT protein, which is a member of the solute carrier family 7 of light-subunit amino acid transporters that form heteromeric amino-acid transporters with a heavy subunit (rBAT, encoded by SLC3A1). Because one of the cystinuria genes (SLC7A9) unmistakably encodes a protein that belongs to the family of light subunit amino-acid transporters, the statement is supported by established biomedical consensus.

238256.long_answer:
All four conditions are intestinal helminthiases produced by roundworms (nematodes):
• Ascariasis is caused by Ascaris lumbricoides, a large intestinal roundworm belonging to the phylum Nematoda.
• Trichuriasis is produced by Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), also a nematode.
• Hookworm disease results from infection with Ancylostoma duodenale or Necator americanus, both hookworms that are nematodes.
• Strongyloidiasis is due to Strongyloides stercoralis (and occasionally other Strongyloides species), likewise classified as nematodes.
These etiologic agents are all in the class Secernentea (formerly Nematoda) and share similar biological features such as a cylindrical, unsegmented body and a complete digestive tract. Therefore, the statement that ascariasis, trichuriasis, hookworm disease, and strongyloidiasis are all caused by nematode infections is consistent with established parasitology consensus.

918946.long_answer: The peptide hormone classically elevated in parathyroid carcinoma is parathyroid hormone (PTH). The PTH gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 11 (11p15.3). Hence, chromosome 11 contains the gene encoding this hormone.

328731.long_answer: The KIND1 gene encodes kindlin-1, a focal-adhesion protein that binds the cytoplasmic tails of β-integrins and couples these extracellular-matrix receptors to the actin cytoskeleton. Thus, kindlin-1 mediates interactions between the extracellular matrix and the key cytoskeletal protein actin.

513351.long_answer: The CPS1 gene encodes mitochondrial carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase I, the first and rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle that produces carbamoyl phosphate from ammonia and bicarbonate. Autosomal-recessive loss-of-function mutations in CPS1 block this step, causing carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase I deficiency, a urea-cycle disorder characterized by dangerously elevated blood ammonia levels (hyperammonemia).

112756.long_answer: Peutz–Jeghers syndrome confers a substantial lifetime risk of colorectal carcinoma—reported around 30–40%—because germ-line STK11/LKB1 mutations drive widespread gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps that can undergo malignant transformation. In contrast, Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome) has a much lower reported colorectal cancer risk (generally <15%), with its cancer burden focused on breast, thyroid, and endometrium. Hence, Peutz–Jeghers carries the higher risk of colorectal malignancy.

821872.long_answer: In the human genome the two Cockayne-syndrome repair genes are situated on different chromosomes: ERCC8 (also known as CSA) maps to chromosome 5q12–q13, whereas ERCC6 (also known as CSB) maps to chromosome 10q11.23. Because they are located on distinct chromosomes (chromosomes 5 and 10, respectively), they are not on the same chromosome.

858680.long_answer: Cockayne syndrome type B is caused by mutations in the ERCC6 gene (also called CSB), which is situated on the long arm of chromosome 10 (cytogenetic band 10q11).

708555.long_answer: Hay-Wells (AEC) syndrome is caused by mutations in the TP63 gene, which encodes the p63 transcription factor. Numerous immunohistochemical and gene-expression studies of squamous cell carcinomas have shown that p63, especially the ΔNp63 isoform, is markedly up-regulated in malignant squamous epithelium. In the vulva specifically, studies (e.g., ‘p63 expression in vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma’, Mod Pathol 2001; ‘ΔNp63 over-expression in vulvar squamous cell carcinoma’, Gynecol Oncol 2004) reported strong, diffuse nuclear p63 staining in the majority of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma samples, whereas adjacent normal epithelium shows much lower or more restricted expression. This pattern is interpreted as over-expression of the p63 protein in vulvar SCC. Therefore, the protein encoded by the gene linked to Hay-Wells syndrome (p63 from TP63) has indeed been observed to be overexpressed in vulvar squamous cell carcinoma.

401433.long_answer: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is caused by germ-line mutations in the tumor-suppressor gene TP53, which is located at 17p13.1 on chromosome 17. Loss of normal TP53 function predisposes carriers to multiple cancers, including the early-onset breast cancers that account for about 4 % of cases in women under 30.

226024.long_answer:
Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) is primarily a disorder of older adults. Epidemiologic studies from Europe, North America and Asia consistently place its point-prevalence in the range of roughly 0.2 – 2 % among community-dwelling persons aged ≥65 years (≈1–20 cases per 1,000 elderly individuals, depending on diagnostic criteria).

Congenital hydrocephalus, in contrast, originates in infancy with an incidence of about 0.5–1.0 per 1,000 live births. Although many affected infants now survive into adulthood, the absolute number that reach late life is small; population-based studies show the prevalence of congenital hydrocephalus in the general population to be on the order of a few per 100,000, and far lower in cohorts aged ≥65 years because of earlier mortality and because most of the population was never affected to begin with.

Therefore, when we look specifically at people aged 65 years or older, NPH is far more common than congenital hydrocephalus. The statement that NPH is estimated to have a higher prevalence rate in this age group than congenital hydrocephalus is consistent with established epidemiologic data.

907848.long_answer: Dissociative (psychogenic) amnesia is, by definition, a loss of autobiographical memories that occurs in the absence of structural brain injury; routine neuroimaging is usually normal and the condition is attributed to psychological mechanisms such as severe stress or trauma. Although retrograde amnesia is most often described after identifiable brain damage (e.g., head trauma, hypoxia, encephalitis), a well-documented subset termed psychogenic or functional retrograde amnesia also exists. In these cases people lose access to past episodic or personal semantic memories without any demonstrable anatomical lesion on MRI or CT; the etiology is likewise psychological. Therefore both dissociative amnesia and a psychogenic form of retrograde amnesia can—and occasionally do—occur in the absence of detectable structural brain damage, making the statement accurate.

326041.long_answer: Grebe-type chondrodysplasia is an autosomal-recessive skeletal dysplasia caused by loss-of-function mutations in the GDF5 (CDMP1) gene. It produces pronounced acromesomelic shortening and malformation of the limbs while the trunk and head remain comparatively normal in size. Because the limbs are disproportionately short relative to the rest of the body, the condition results in disproportionate dwarfism rather than proportionate dwarfism.

823605.long_answer: Bacterial vaginosis is indeed a vaginal infection linked to an over-growth and imbalance of vaginal bacteria (e.g., Gardnerella and other anaerobes). In contrast, a vaginal yeast infection—properly called vulvovaginal candidiasis—is caused by an overgrowth of Candida species, which are fungi (yeasts), not bacteria. Therefore, while both conditions are vaginal infections, only bacterial vaginosis is caused by excessive bacterial growth; a yeast infection is caused by fungal overgrowth. Hence the statement is incorrect.

308865.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene are well-established as the cause of Marfan syndrome and several other fibrillin-1–related connective-tissue disorders. Although people with Marfan syndrome can develop postural kyphosis or kyphoscoliosis as a secondary skeletal manifestation, FBN1 mutations have not been implicated in the distinct condition called juvenile osteochondrosis of the spine (Scheuermann juvenile kyphosis). Scheuermann disease is classified as a developmental disorder of the vertebral end-plates; its genetic basis remains uncertain and, to date, no reproducible association with FBN1 has been demonstrated in either linkage studies, candidate-gene analyses, or genome-wide studies. Consequently, current medical consensus does not link FBN1 to the form of kyphosis classified as juvenile osteochondrosis of the spine.

610243.long_answer: Sarcoma botryoides is a subtype of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma that classically arises in the vagina of infants and very young girls (most cases occur in children younger than 5 years). In contrast, primary squamous-cell carcinoma of the vagina is a malignancy that overwhelmingly affects post-menopausal women, with peak incidence in the sixth to eighth decades of life. It is rare in the pediatric population. Therefore, while sarcoma botryoides is most common in infants and young children, squamous-cell carcinoma of the vagina is not, making the statement incorrect.

464739.long_answer: Triple-A (Allgrove) syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AAAS gene, which encodes the nuclear-pore-complex protein ALADIN. When ALADIN is absent or mis-localized, a subset of proteins that normally use the nuclear pore for import cannot enter the nucleus efficiently. Several independent studies of patient-derived fibroblasts and ALADIN-knock-down cell lines have shown that two DNA-repair factors—aprataxin (APTX) and DNA ligase I (LIG1)—are among the cargos whose nuclear import is impaired. These proteins accumulate in the cytoplasm instead of the nucleus, resulting in defective repair of single-strand DNA breaks and increased sensitivity to oxidative damage. Hence, the AAAS mutation responsible for Triple-A syndrome does indeed lead to reduced nuclear import of aprataxin and DNA ligase I, both of which are components of the DNA-repair machinery.

674571.long_answer: The GJB3 gene, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin-31 and is implicated in Erythrokeratodermia variabilis, is situated on the short arm of human chromosome 1 (region 1p34–p35).

696503.long_answer: Mutations in the CEP63 gene (centrosomal protein 63 kDa) have been shown to cause Seckel syndrome. The CEP63 protein localises to centrosomes and is predicted to contain six distinct coiled-coil domains, a structural feature highlighted in the original genetic studies linking CEP63 loss-of-function mutations to the microcephaly and dwarfism characteristic of Seckel syndrome.

905430.long_answer: The enzyme that converts adenosine to inosine in humans is adenosine deaminase (ADA). The ADA gene is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 20, at cytogenetic band 20q13.12. This locus encodes the ADA protein that deaminates adenosine (and deoxyadenosine) to inosine, a key reaction in purine metabolism; loss-of-function mutations cause ADA-deficient severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).

488726.long_answer: Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) is encoded by the BTK gene situated on the long arm of the X chromosome (region Xq21.3-Xq22). Mutations in this X-linked gene disrupt BTK function and cause X-linked agammaglobulinemia, confirming that the responsible gene resides on the X chromosome.

774492.long_answer: Glycogen storage disease type Ib is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC37A4 gene. SLC37A4 encodes the endoplasmic-reticulum glucose-6-phosphate translocase (G6PT); when this transporter is defective, glucose-6-phosphate cannot be shuttled into the ER lumen for hydrolysis by glucose-6-phosphatase, resulting in the metabolic abnormalities characteristic of GSD-Ib.

634992.long_answer: Mohr–Tranebjærg syndrome (also called deafness-dystonia syndrome) is caused by pathogenic variants in the TIMM8A (DDP1) gene. TIMM8A is located on the short arm of the X chromosome at Xp22. Mutations here lead to the X-linked recessive transmission pattern characteristic of the syndrome.

585005.long_answer: Urbach–Wiethe disease (lipoid proteinosis) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ECM1 gene. ECM1 encodes extracellular matrix protein 1, a secreted protein whose domains contain tandem repeat motifs rich in cysteine residues arranged in a characteristic pattern. Defects in ECM1 disrupt normal extracellular matrix organization, leading to the mucocutaneous and neurological manifestations of the disease.

685009.long_answer: Lipoid proteinosis (Urbach–Wiethe disease) is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ECM1 gene, which encodes extracellular matrix protein 1. Defective ECM1 leads to abnormal deposition of hyaline material in skin and mucosa and to characteristic symmetrical calcifications of the medial temporal lobes, especially the amygdala, seen on neuroimaging.

345808.long_answer: Sanfilippo syndrome type B (MPS III B) results from mutations in the NAGLU gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme α-N-acetylglucosaminidase. This enzyme degrades heparan sulfate by hydrolyzing terminal N-acetyl-D-glucosamine residues in N-acetyl-α-D-glucosaminides; loss of its activity produces the clinical picture of MPS-III type B.

547887.long_answer: Sanfilippo syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type III) has four main subtypes (A–D), each caused by deficiency of a distinct enzyme in heparan-sulfate degradation. Mutations in the HGSNAT gene, which encodes Heparan-α-glucosaminide N-acetyltransferase, lead specifically to the enzymatic deficiency defining Sanfilippo syndrome type C (MPS IIIC).

144512.long_answer: Tibial hemimelia-polysyndactyly-triphalangeal thumb syndrome has been genetically linked to sequence variants or genomic rearrangements encompassing the limb-specific Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) enhancer (the ZRS) that lies within intron 5 of the LMBR1 gene on chromosome 7q36. Both LMBR1 itself (whose full name is “limb development membrane protein 1”) and, more importantly, the ZRS enhancer that it harbors are critical regulators of SHH expression in the early limb bud—the signaling center that establishes the anterior-posterior (thumb-to-little-finger) axis of developing limbs. Disruption of this regulatory element or the surrounding gene region alters SHH signaling, leading to malformations such as tibial hemimelia, preaxial polydactyly, and triphalangeal thumb. Because the causative locus functions specifically in patterning and growth of the embryonic limb, it is considered to be directly involved in limb development according to well-established developmental biology and clinical genetics literature.

984826.long_answer: The Alström syndrome gene ALMS1 encodes a centrosome/basal-body protein essential for primary cilium formation. siRNA knock-down of ALMS1 in cultured cells abolishes or severely shortens the primary cilium, demonstrating that loss of ALMS1 causes defective primary ciliogenesis— the cellular defect underlying Alström syndrome.

897214.long_answer: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT) is most frequently caused by mutations in the RYR2 gene, which encodes the cardiac ryanodine receptor type-2 (RyR2) calcium-release channel. Multiple biochemical and functional studies (e.g., pull-down assays, co-immunoprecipitation, surface-plasmon resonance, and single-channel recordings) have demonstrated that the Ca2+-binding protein sorcin (gene symbol SRI) binds directly to cytoplasmic domains of RyR2 and modulates its channel activity. This RyR2–sorcin interaction is considered part of the normal regulation of sarcoplasmic-reticulum Ca2+ release in cardiomyocytes. Therefore, the protein encoded by the gene most commonly linked to CPVT (RyR2) does indeed interact with the sorcin protein.

926927.long_answer: The cardiac ryanodine receptor gene is RYR2, which encodes the Ca²⁺ release channel of the sarcoplasmic reticulum in heart muscle. Mutations in RYR2 are a well-established cause of catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT). The RYR2 gene is located on chromosome 1 (region 1q42.1-q43).

816884.long_answer:
The vitamin-K–dependent Protein S that is deficient in the inherited thrombophilia called “protein S deficiency” is a coagulation co-factor encoded by the PROS1 gene; it serves mainly as a co-factor for activated protein C in down-regulating factors Va and VIIIa.  

The molecule that blocks insertion of the membrane attack complex (MAC) during complement activation is vitronectin, a plasma glycoprotein historically referred to as “S-protein” in the complement literature. Vitronectin is encoded by the VTN gene and is structurally and functionally unrelated to the anticoagulant Protein S.  

Thus the anticoagulant Protein S and the MAC-inhibitory vitronectin (complement “S-protein”) are two distinct proteins that share an old name but are not the same molecule.

808020.long_answer: Acyl-CoA oxidase deficiency is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ACOX1 gene, which encodes the peroxisomal very-long-chain acyl-CoA oxidase. The ACOX1 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 17q25 on human chromosome 17; therefore, the gene responsible for this disorder is located on chromosome 17.

874633.long_answer: Carey-Fineman-Ziter syndrome is produced by recessive mutations in the MYMK (myomaker/TMEM8C) gene, which encodes a muscle-specific membrane protein that drives myoblast fusion during skeletal-muscle development. The human MYMK gene is situated on chromosome 9 (cytogenetic band 9p13.3), so the disease-associated locus lies on chromosome 9.

841632.long_answer: The human GBE1 gene, encoding the glycogen-branching enzyme whose loss-of-function mutations cause Glycogen Storage Disease Type IV (Andersen disease), is mapped to chromosome 3 (locus 3p12.3).

773528.long_answer: Down syndrome results from trisomy of chromosome 21, an extra copy of all or part of chromosome 21. Microtia—the under-development or absence of the external ear—is typically sporadic or part of other craniofacial syndromes (e.g., Treacher-Collins, Goldenhar), and its etiology is multifactorial (genetic variants, vascular disruption, environmental factors such as maternal retinoid or diabetes). It is not linked to trisomy 21. Although children with Down syndrome can have small, low-set ears, the specific congenital malformation termed microtia is neither characteristic of nor caused by the chromosomal abnormality that produces Down syndrome. Therefore, the statement is incorrect.

426619.long_answer:
Lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs) are a group of inherited metabolic disorders in which deficiency of a lysosomal enzyme or associated protein leads to accumulation of undegraded substrates within lysosomes.  

• Mucolipidosis type I (also called sialidosis) is caused by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme neuraminidase (NEU1). As a result, sialyl-rich oligosaccharides and glycoproteins accumulate in lysosomes. Mucolipidoses (types I–IV) are universally classified within the lysosomal storage disease family.  

• Glycogen storage disease type II (Pompe disease) results from deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme acid α-glucosidase (acid maltase). This leads to intralysosomal accumulation of glycogen and progressive cellular dysfunction. Although it is also grouped with glycogen storage disorders, it is explicitly included in standard lists of lysosomal storage diseases because the primary defect and substrate accumulation occur in lysosomes.  

Therefore, both ML I (sialidosis) and Pompe disease are recognized members of the lysosomal storage disease group, so the statement is correct.

142159.long_answer: The two most frequent mutation classes in nemaline myopathy occur in the NEB and ACTA1 genes. NEB encodes nebulin, a gigantic sarcomeric protein that runs along the length of the thin filament in skeletal muscle. Nebulin acts as a ‘molecular ruler’, with its size scaling in proportion to the length of the actin‐based thin filament. Thus, the NEB gene matches both criteria in the question.

252236.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal-dominant connective-tissue disorder produced by pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene, which encodes fibrillin-1. The weakened aortic media in Marfan patients predisposes them to life-threatening aortic aneurysm and acute aortic dissection—a cardiovascular emergency that typically manifests with the abrupt onset of severe, tearing chest or back pain.

221274.long_answer:
The SERPINA1 gene encodes the serine protease inhibitor alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT). Pathogenic variants in SERPINA1 (most commonly the Z allele [Glu342Lys] and, less frequently, the S allele [Glu264Val] and numerous null alleles) reduce the production or functional activity of AAT in the bloodstream and lung tissue. AAT’s normal role is to inhibit neutrophil elastase and other proteases that can degrade alveolar walls. When AAT levels are markedly reduced (< 11 µM, roughly < 57 mg/dL), unchecked elastase activity leads to progressive destruction of alveolar septa, producing panacinar emphysema—often at a younger age and with a basilar predominance compared with smoking-related centrilobular emphysema.

Large epidemiologic studies, familial aggregation data, and mechanistic research have established alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency as a well-accepted genetic risk factor for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), particularly emphysema. Clinical guidelines from organizations such as the American Thoracic Society, European Respiratory Society, and World Health Organization recommend testing for SERPINA1 mutations in individuals with unexplained emphysema or COPD, underscoring the consensus that these mutations confer significant susceptibility.

Therefore, mutations in SERPINA1 that lower functional alpha-1 antitrypsin levels are definitively recognized as genetic risk factors for emphysema.

271344.long_answer: The condition involving excessive elastin degradation from protease–antiprotease imbalance is α-1 antitrypsin deficiency, caused by mutations in the SERPINA1 gene encoding α-1 antitrypsin. After the 24-residue signal peptide is cleaved, the secreted (mature) α-1 antitrypsin polypeptide consists of 394 amino acids.

547348.long_answer: Endodermal sinus (yolk sac) tumors secrete alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). The AFP gene, which encodes this secreted protein, is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 4 (region 4q13).

999464.long_answer: Humans selectively retain the α-tocopherol form of vitamin E because hepatic α-tocopherol transfer protein (α-TTP) preferentially incorporates it into circulating lipoproteins. The α-TTP protein is encoded by the TTPA gene, which is located on chromosome 8 (region 8q13).

295652.long_answer: Sotos syndrome is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the NSD1 gene. NSD1 is located in the 5q35 chromosomal region, so the causative gene for Sotos syndrome resides on chromosome 5.

864685.long_answer: X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita with adrenal insufficiency and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is caused by mutations in the DAX1 (NR0B1) gene. DAX1 encodes an orphan nuclear receptor that is unique in the family because it lacks the classical C4 zinc-finger DNA-binding domain present in most nuclear receptors, yet still modulates transcription to control adrenal and testicular development.

812733.long_answer:
Classical phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase. When untreated it primarily produces neurological damage ‑ intellectual disability, seizures, behavioral problems – but it does not typically cause intrinsic liver failure or cirrhosis.  

Tyrosinemia type 1 is caused by deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase. Accumulation of toxic metabolites (fumarylacetoacetate, succinyl-acetone) produces progressive hepatic injury beginning in infancy, leading to acute liver failure, chronic cirrhosis, and a markedly increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma if nitisinone therapy or liver transplantation is not provided.  

Because severe liver disease is a characteristic, frequent, and life-threatening complication of untreated tyrosinemia type 1 but is not a feature of untreated classical PKU, tyrosinemia type 1 is indeed far more likely to result in severe liver disease when left untreated.

130827.long_answer: In tyrosinemia, the amino acid tyrosine accumulates because its catabolic pathway is defective. Tyrosine is normally produced endogenously from phenylalanine via phenylalanine hydroxylase. In phenylketonuria—a genetic disorder caused by deficiency of this enzyme—the catabolism of phenylalanine is blocked, preventing the conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine. Consequently, tyrosine can no longer be synthesized in adequate amounts and becomes conditionally essential. Thus, the disorder that makes tyrosine essential impairs the breakdown of phenylalanine.

900303.long_answer: Among the oral potentially malignant disorders, erythroplakia shows the highest prevalence of severe epithelial dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, or early invasive squamous-cell carcinoma at the time of biopsy. Reported malignant-transformation rates for erythroplakia range from 30 % to well over 50 %, whereas the corresponding figures for oral leukoplakia are generally in the 1–5 % (occasionally up to 15 %) range over several years of follow-up. Because squamous-cell carcinoma is by far the most common histologic type of head and neck cancer, these data mean that an erythroplakic lesion is substantially more likely than a leukoplakic lesion to evolve into (or already harbor) head-and-neck squamous-cell carcinoma. This relationship is well-documented in oral pathology and oncology guidelines, so the statement is consistent with established biomedical consensus.

943668.long_answer: The gene described is SOX2, a transcription factor critical for maintaining embryonic stem-cell pluripotency and for normal neural and eye development; pathogenic SOX2 mutations cause bilateral anophthalmia. The canonical human SOX2 protein comprises 317 amino acids.

484452.long_answer: Raynaud episodes are termed secondary when they occur in association with an identifiable underlying disorder. Cryoglobulinemia causes cold-precipitable immunoglobulins that obstruct small vessels, producing the digital numbness and color changes typical of Raynaud attacks. Because the Raynaud manifestations arise as a consequence of this systemic disease, they are classified as secondary rather than primary (idiopathic) Raynaud phenomenon.

436577.long_answer:
Many primary mitochondrial disorders arise from pathogenic mutations in nuclear- or mitochondrial-encoded subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) system—Complexes I, III, IV and V—or in the assembly factors that help build these complexes. Complexes I, III and IV are the proton-pumping enzymes that move H⁺ from the matrix into the inter-membrane space, establishing the electrochemical proton gradient (proton-motive force). Complex V (ATP synthase) then uses that gradient to make ATP.

When mutations impair the ability of any of these complexes to pump protons efficiently, or to allow controlled proton flow back through ATP synthase, the gradient is weakened or lost, ATP synthesis falls, and cellular energy deficiency ensues. This biochemical defect underlies numerous mitochondrial diseases such as Leigh syndrome (mutations in NDUFS/NDUFV genes of Complex I, SURF1 assembly factor for Complex IV, etc.), mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis, many forms of mitochondrial myopathy, neuropathy, and cardiomyopathy. Thus, interference with proton-gradient formation is a well-established pathogenic mechanism in mitochondrial disease.

542627.long_answer: The electron transport chain (respiratory chain) that produces most cellular ATP in eukaryotes is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Disorders that impair this chain—collectively termed mitochondrial respiratory chain or oxidative phosphorylation disorders—arise from dysfunction of the mitochondrion, the organelle responsible for aerobic energy production.

991912.long_answer: The HPSE2 gene, located on chromosome 10q24–q25, encodes the human enzyme Heparanase-2. Biallelic (autosomal-recessive) loss-of-function mutations in HPSE2 cause Urofacial Syndrome (UFS), a disorder in which affected children develop bladder dysfunction and a characteristic inverted facial expression that resembles crying when they attempt to smile.

488399.long_answer: The HMGCL gene, situated on chromosome 1p36, encodes mitochondrial 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase. This enzyme catalyzes the cleavage of HMG-CoA to acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA, the terminal reaction of hepatic ketogenesis. The same reaction is also a critical step in the intramitochondrial degradation pathway of the branched-chain amino acid leucine, making HMGCL essential for both ketone-body formation and leucine catabolism.

894544.long_answer: Several well-described ectodermal-dysplasia syndromes are produced by mutations in the PVRL1 and PVRL4 genes, which encode the cell-adhesion molecules nectin-1 and nectin-4, respectively. Nectins are members of the immunoglobulin superfamily of cell-adhesion molecules (IgSF CAMs). Loss-of-function variants in PVRL1 cause Cleft Lip/Palate-Ectodermal Dysplasia syndrome (also called ectodermal dysplasia-syndactyly syndrome type 1), while PVRL4 mutations cause ectodermal dysplasia-syndactyly syndrome type 2. Thus, a form of ectodermal dysplasia is indeed associated with mutations in a gene that encodes an IgSF CAM protein.

881321.long_answer: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is a rare inherited bleeding disorder produced by quantitative or qualitative deficiency of the platelet membrane glycoprotein Ib-V-IX complex—the receptor for von Willebrand factor, the large multimeric glycoprotein that mediates primary platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelium. Loss of this receptor impairs vWF-dependent platelet plug formation, leading to mucocutaneous bleeding and thrombocytopenia characteristic of the syndrome.

196497.long_answer: Type 2A Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts is caused by recessive mutations in the HEPACAM (GLIALCAM) gene, which is mapped to cytogenetic band 11q24 on chromosome 11.

272275.long_answer: Dubin–Johnson syndrome is characterized by a grossly black or darkly pigmented liver due to the accumulation of polymerized epinephrine metabolites in hepatocytes. Rotor syndrome, although clinically similar in that both disorders cause a predominantly conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia without significant liver dysfunction, does not show this hepatic pigmentation—liver histology in Rotor syndrome is essentially normal in color. Therefore, black liver pigmentation is not a feature shared by both conditions and is not part of their common symptom set.

121722.long_answer: Alglucerase (Ceredase) was the first FDA-approved enzyme replacement therapy, used to treat Gaucher disease. Gaucher disease results from mutations in the GBA gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme β-glucocerebrosidase. The GBA gene is situated on the long arm of chromosome 1 (1q21–q22), so the causal mutations occur on chromosome 1.

211369.long_answer: Smith–Fineman–Myers syndrome (catalogued as X-linked intellectual-disability, Smith-Fineman-Myers type; MRX-SMF) is caused by pathogenic variants in the ATRX gene located on Xq13.3. The ATRX protein is a member of the SWI/SNF family of chromatin-remodelling proteins and possesses a characteristic C-terminal SNF2-type ATP-dependent helicase/ATPase domain that is essential for its chromatin-remodelling activity. Hence, the X-chromosomal gene whose mutation produces Smith–Fineman–Myers syndrome does indeed encode a protein containing an ATPase/helicase domain.

639775.long_answer: The hereditary lymphedema described by William F. Milroy in 1892 (Milroy disease) is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the FLT4 gene (encoding VEGFR-3). FLT4 is situated at cytogenetic band 5q35.3 on chromosome 5; thus the disease-causing mutation resides on chromosome 5. The condition typically presents with congenital, often unilateral, lower-extremity lymphedema and can be associated with scrotal edema or hydrocele in affected males.

860205.long_answer: BK virus is a member of the Polyomaviridae family. Like other polyomaviruses, its small, circular double-stranded DNA genome has an “early region” that encodes the viral regulatory proteins called T antigens. The main early protein, the large T antigen, interacts with cellular tumor-suppressor proteins such as pRb and p53. By inactivating pRb, large T antigen releases E2F transcription factors, thereby driving quiescent host cells from G₁ into S phase so that the cellular DNA-synthesis machinery becomes available for viral DNA replication. Thus, the BK-virus genome does indeed encode a protein whose established function is to regulate (promote) the transition of infected cells into the S phase of the cell cycle.

745864.long_answer:
The classic form of familial amyloid polyneuropathy (ATTR-FAP) results from pathogenic variants in the transthyretin (TTR) gene, which is located on chromosome 18 (band 18q12.1).  
Erythropoietic protoporphyria is most frequently caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ferrochelatase (FECH) gene, situated on chromosome 18 at 18q21.3 (a less common X-linked form involves ALAS2 on the X chromosome, but the canonical autosomal form maps to FECH on chromosome 18).  
Because both TTR and FECH reside on chromosome 18, the genes responsible for familial amyloid polyneuropathy and the common autosomal form of erythropoietic protoporphyria are indeed located on the same chromosome. Hence, the statement is supported by established genetic evidence.

493214.long_answer: Hereditary spherocytosis is a genetic red-cell membrane defect that produces spherical erythrocytes prone to splenic destruction. The accelerated hemolysis releases large amounts of unconjugated bilirubin, producing the pre-hepatic category known as hemolytic jaundice.

508708.long_answer: Keppen-Lubinsky syndrome is an exceptionally rare congenital neurodevelopmental disorder produced by de novo heterozygous missense mutations in KCNJ6, the gene that encodes the G protein-activated inward-rectifier potassium channel 2 (GIRK2). Disruption of GIRK2 channel function underlies the syndrome’s characteristic craniofacial, lipodystrophic, and severe developmental features, establishing the direct causal link between the KCNJ6 mutation and the disease.

190359.long_answer: In November 2024 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved acoramidis, an oral transthyretin tetramer stabilizer. By preventing transthyretin misfolding and amyloid deposition, the drug treats transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy—a restrictive cardiomyopathy that develops when amyloidosis infiltrates the myocardium.

791568.long_answer: Lenz microphthalmia syndrome (designated MCOPS2 in the syndromic microphthalmia series) is produced by pathogenic variants in the BCOR gene. BCOR encodes the corepressor of the POZ/BTB-zinc-finger transcription factor BCL6, a regulator that is crucial for normal development of the secondary palate (roof of the mouth). Loss of BCOR function disrupts this BCL6-dependent transcriptional repression, leading to the characteristic microphthalmia together with cleft palate and multiple other non-ocular malformations that define the syndrome.

623929.long_answer: Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the CTSC gene, which encodes the lysosomal cysteine protease cathepsin C (also called dipeptidyl-peptidase I). Cathepsin C is an amino-terminal exopeptidase: it sequentially removes dipeptides from the free N-terminus of proteins and peptides. It does not cleave dipeptides from the C-terminus. Therefore, the statement that the PLS-associated gene catalyzes excision of dipeptides from the C-terminus is incorrect.

215035.long_answer: Temporally graded retrograde amnesia is a hallmark of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, an amnestic disorder that arises from chronic deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B1). Lack of thiamine impairs glucose metabolism in diencephalic and hippocampal circuits, producing profound anterograde amnesia with a retrograde gradient; thus vitamin B1 is the critical factor linked to this syndrome.

728207.long_answer:
Enzyme deficiencies that impair the urea cycle (e.g., ornithine-transcarbamylase, carbamyl-phosphate synthetase, argininosuccinate-lyase deficiencies) lead to hyperammonemia because ammonia cannot be incorporated into urea. Standard, evidence-based therapy for these disorders consists of protein restriction, intravenous glucose/lipids to reduce catabolism, ammonia-scavenger drugs such as sodium benzoate, sodium phenylacetate/phenylbutyrate, supplementation with arginine or citrulline, and, in severe cases, hemodialysis or liver transplantation. 

Medications developed for diabetes management (insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas, GLP-1 agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors, etc.) act on glucose homeostasis pathways and have no pharmacologic effect on the deficient urea-cycle enzymes or on ammonia detoxification. They are therefore not used to alleviate the symptoms of hyperammonemia caused by these enzyme defects, and in some circumstances (e.g., metformin in hepatic compromise) could worsen the clinical picture. Consequently, current medical consensus does not support the use of diabetes medications for treating conditions in which an enzyme deficiency causes excess ammonia.

728709.long_answer:
The interval from the onset of ventricular depolarisation (start of the QRS complex) to the end of ventricular repolarisation (end of the T wave) is the QT interval.  Because the QT duration varies with heart rate, the value used clinically is the corrected QT (QTc).  In adults, a QTc up to about 440 ms in men and 460 ms in women is generally regarded as normal; values above ~450 ms in men or ~470 ms in women are considered prolonged, and a QTc ≥480 ms on serial tracings or ≥500 ms on any single tracing strongly supports the diagnosis of Long QT syndrome (LQTS).

An uncorrected QT of 400–450 ms at resting heart rates near 60 beats min⁻¹ usually corresponds to a QTc that is within the normal or at most borderline range, not definitively prolonged.  Therefore, a ventricular contraction-to-relaxation time of 400–450 ms, by itself, is not sufficient evidence to diagnose Long QT syndrome; additional information (exact heart rate, QTc calculation, clinical context, genetic testing) would be required.

654787.long_answer: Keratitis–ichthyosis–deafness (KID) syndrome is most commonly caused by dominant missense mutations in the GJB2 gene, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin-26. GJB2 is located on the long arm of human chromosome 13 at band 13q11-q12, so the gene—and the pathogenic mutations that produce KID syndrome—reside on chromosome 13.

250141.long_answer: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive fibrosing interstitial pneumonia that predominantly affects adults over 50 years of age and carries a median survival of only 3–5 years. Like chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, IPF presents with exertional dyspnea, persistent dry cough, bibasilar crackles, and a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern of fibrosis on high-resolution CT. Because the clinical and imaging features overlap, distinguishing IPF from chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis is critical for appropriate management and prognostication.

728820.long_answer: Both black piedra (caused by the dematiaceous fungus Piedraia hortae) and white piedra (caused predominantly by Trichosporon species) are infections limited to the hair shaft. Because the fungi reside on and within the hair shaft itself, definitive eradication is achieved most reliably by physically removing the infected hair. Standard dermatology and infectious-disease texts list clipping or shaving of the affected hairs as the primary, often curative, measure for both conditions; topical or systemic antifungals are considered adjuncts or alternatives only when cosmetic or practical reasons preclude shaving. Therefore, shaving (or closely clipping) the involved hair is regarded as a necessary component of effective treatment for both black and white piedra.

184050.long_answer:
Peroxisomal acyl-coenzyme A oxidase 1 is the first, rate-limiting enzyme of the peroxisomal β-oxidation pathway. It is produced from the human ACOX1 gene located on chromosome 17q25. Pathogenic variants in ACOX1 abolish or markedly reduce enzyme activity and give rise to the autosomal-recessive disorder classically called peroxisomal acyl-CoA oxidase deficiency or pseudo-neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy (OMIM 264470).  

Because the biochemical hallmark of the disease (marked accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids and absent ACOX1 activity) can be measured in cultured chorionic-villus or amniotic-fluid cells, families at risk can obtain a molecular or enzymatic prenatal diagnosis. After birth, the condition is usually identified in the neonatal period or early infancy through VLCFA analysis, enzyme assay in fibroblasts, or ACOX1 gene sequencing.  

Thus, peroxisomal acyl-coenzyme A oxidase 1 is indeed an enzyme encoded by a gene whose pathogenic variants cause a disease that can be diagnosed either prenatally or postnatally.

335715.long_answer: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) is a rare autosomal dominant vascular dysplasia characterized by mucocutaneous telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) in organs such as the lungs and liver. Large visceral AVMs create low-resistance shunts that markedly increase cardiac output, predisposing affected patients to high-output or congestive cardiac failure.

506743.long_answer: Current genetic studies show that most cases of Maffucci syndrome carry somatic (mosaic) gain-of-function mutations in the isocitrate dehydrogenase genes IDH1 and IDH2. IDH1 is located on chromosome 2q33.3, whereas IDH2 is located on chromosome 15q26.1. No commonly-implicated Maffucci-syndrome gene resides on chromosome 13. Therefore the statement that the genes most commonly associated with Maffucci syndrome are on chromosomes 2 and 13 is not consistent with the established scientific consensus.

531534.long_answer: Lysinuric protein intolerance is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC7A7 gene. This gene encodes the cationic amino acid transporter y+L-type amino acid transporter 1 (y+LAT-1), which, as part of the y+L system heterodimer, mediates export of cationic amino acids (lysine, arginine, ornithine) from epithelial and immune cells. Defective y+LAT-1 impairs renal and intestinal reabsorption of these amino acids, producing the clinical features of the disease.

174363.long_answer: Cystathionine β-synthase (CBS) catalyzes the pyridoxal-phosphate–dependent condensation of homocysteine with serine to form cystathionine. Inherited deficiency of CBS causes classical homocystinuria, characterized by elevated homocysteine and methionine levels and clinical findings involving connective tissue, skeleton, eyes, and vascular system.

637389.long_answer: Although juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is an autoimmune-mediated inflammatory arthritis of childhood and osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease that usually affects older adults, several clinical manifestations overlap. Both conditions can present with joint pain (arthralgia), morning or inactivity-related stiffness, limited range of motion, and functional impairment of the affected joints. The underlying pathophysiology, age of onset, and presence of systemic inflammatory signs differ, but the symptomatic overlap of pain and stiffness means the two disorders do share some symptoms.

365940.long_answer: Angel-shaped phalango-epiphyseal dysplasia is caused by pathogenic variants in the GDF5 (CDMP1) gene. GDF5 encodes Growth Differentiation Factor 5, a TGF-β superfamily protein that is highly homologous to bone morphogenetic proteins. Genetic and linkage studies have mapped GDF5 to cytogenetic band 20q11.2, establishing that the responsible gene resides on chromosome 20.

662928.long_answer:
Psittacosis is a zoonotic infection caused by Chlamydophila (Chlamydia) psittaci acquired from birds. In humans it most commonly manifests as an "atypical" community-acquired pneumonia and is listed in medical texts alongside Mycoplasma and Chlamydophila pneumoniae as classic atypical pneumonia pathogens.

The respiratory illness first recognized among attendees of the 1976 American Legion convention in Philadelphia was Legionnaires’ disease, produced by the bacterium Legionella pneumophila. Legionella species are likewise prototypical causes of atypical pneumonia; the term "Legionella pneumonia" is often used interchangeably with "atypical pneumonia" in differential-diagnosis tables.

Because both psittacosis and Legionnaires’ disease are universally categorized in standard infectious-disease references as etiologies of atypical pneumonia, the statement is supported by established biomedical consensus.

413039.long_answer: The commonest genetic cause of malignant hyperthermia is mutation of the RYR1 gene, which is located on the long arm of chromosome 19 (19q13.2). Chromosome 19 is well known for having the highest gene density in the human genome; most reference annotations list roughly 1,400–1,600 protein-coding genes on this chromosome, often summarized as “about 1,500 genes.” Because chromosome 19 both carries the principal malignant-hyperthermia gene (RYR1) and is recognised as the most gene-rich human chromosome with ~1,500 genes, the statement is consistent with established scientific consensus.

450407.long_answer: Among the seven classical Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) complementation groups, the gene whose mutations can produce either the XP phenotype alone or, alternatively, the neuro-ectodermal disorder trichothiodystrophy (TTD) is the XPD gene (official symbol ERCC2). ERCC2 encodes the DNA helicase component of the TFIIH complex that participates in nucleotide-excision repair. Cytogenetic and sequence mapping place ERCC2/XPD at chromosome band 19q13.32 (chromosome 19, long arm, region 13). This chromosomal location is confirmed in OMIM (Gene ID 2068), NCBI Gene, Ensembl, and numerous genetic studies. Therefore, the XP-associated gene whose mutation can lead to trichothiodystrophy is indeed located on chromosome 19.

121000.long_answer: Glutaric acidemia type 2 (multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency) most commonly results from pathogenic variants in the genes that encode the two subunits of electron-transferring flavoprotein (ETF) or in ETF-ubiquinone oxidoreductase. ETF consists of an α-subunit (gene symbol ETFA) and a β-subunit (gene symbol ETFB). Cytogenetic and physical mapping studies have shown:  • ETFA is located on chromosome 15q23-q25.  • ETFB is located on chromosome 19q13.3. Because disease-causing mutations have been documented in both ETFA and ETFB, and the ETFB gene resides on chromosome 19, it is correct to state that “one of the subunits of the electron-transferring flavoprotein, which is mutated in individuals with glutaric acidemia type 2, is encoded by a gene localized on chromosome 19.”

800131.long_answer: Multicentric carpotarsal osteolysis syndrome (MCTO) is caused by heterozygous missense variants in the transcription factor gene MAFB on chromosome 20q12. In contrast, Winchester syndrome (also called multicentric osteolysis, nodulosis, and arthropathy) is produced by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in genes of the matrix-metalloproteinase pathway—most commonly MMP2 and, in some families, MMP14. Thus the two disorders are linked to entirely different genes and molecular mechanisms, so they are not associated with the same gene.

138185.long_answer: Cystinuria results from defects in the heterodimeric renal amino-acid transporter composed of an rBAT heavy chain (SLC3A1) and a light chain encoded by SLC7A9. The SLC7A9 gene specifically encodes the b(0,+)-type amino acid transporter 1 (b0,+AT1), which mediates reabsorption of cystine and dibasic amino acids in the renal proximal tubules; mutations in SLC7A9 therefore lead to impaired cystine reabsorption and stone-forming cystinuria.

380031.long_answer: Sir Archibald Garrod, an early-20th-century British physician, pioneered the study of hereditary metabolic disorders that he termed “inborn errors of metabolism.” His work laid the foundation for understanding the group of glycogen-storage diseases, including Glycogen storage disease type IV (Andersen disease), which results from a congenital deficiency of the glycogen-branching enzyme.

205338.long_answer: Kindler syndrome is an autosomal-recessive skin fragility disorder that is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the FERMT1 gene (also called KIND1, encoding kindlin-1). In humans FERMT1 resides on chromosome 20, but the mouse orthologue (Fermt1) is mapped to chromosome 2 (cytoband B, ~45 cM; genomic coordinates ≈81 Mb). Because the question asks specifically about the chromosomal location of the gene that, when mutated, causes Kindler syndrome in the mouse genome, the correct chromosomal assignment is indeed chromosome 2. Therefore, the statement is supported by established genomic data.

281682.long_answer: The gene described—TP53, located at 17p13.1 and recognized as the single most commonly mutated gene across human cancers—does figure among the genes known to confer hereditary susceptibility to breast-ovarian cancer. Germ-line (inherited) pathogenic variants of TP53 cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome, a cancer-predisposition disorder in which early-onset breast cancer is one of the hallmark tumors and ovarian cancer risk is also elevated. Because of this, clinical and research gene panels that catalogue hereditary breast–ovarian cancer susceptibility genes routinely list TP53 alongside BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, CHEK2, ATM, RAD51C/D and others. Therefore, the short-arm-of-chromosome-17 gene in question does appear among the accepted genes associated with hereditary breast–ovarian cancer syndrome.

305869.long_answer: Arthrogryposis-renal dysfunction-cholestasis (ARC) syndrome is most commonly caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in the VPS33B gene. VPS33B is mapped to cytogenetic band 15q26.1 on chromosome 15, so the pathogenic gene responsible for ARC syndrome is located on chromosome 15.

972475.long_answer: Large-for-gestational-age (LGA) infants and fetal macrosomia are strongly linked to maternal hyperglycaemia that first appears during pregnancy, i.e., gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). Elevated maternal glucose crosses the placenta, stimulates fetal pancreatic insulin secretion, and drives excessive fetal growth. Clinical guidelines (ACOG, ADA, WHO) list gestational diabetes as one of the principal, well-established risk factors for LGA/macrosomia alongside maternal obesity and excessive gestational weight gain. Therefore, high blood sugar that develops during pregnancy in a woman without pre-existing diabetes is indeed a main risk factor for delivering an LGA or macrosomic baby.

264681.long_answer: Hereditary protein S deficiency results from pathogenic variants in the PROS1 gene, which encodes protein S. The PROS1 gene is mapped to chromosome 3 (band 3q11.2; older literature may cite 3p11-q11). There is no evidence that the causative gene resides on chromosome 10. Therefore, the statement claiming the gene is on chromosome 10 is incorrect.

486131.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal-dominant, multi-system connective-tissue disorder produced by mutations in the FBN1 (fibrillin-1) gene. FBN1 is located at 15q21.1 on chromosome 15, spans approximately 230 kb of genomic DNA, and is composed of 65 coding exons. Pathogenic variants in this gene disrupt fibrillin-1 microfibril formation, leading to the characteristic skeletal, ocular, and cardiovascular manifestations of Marfan syndrome.

362372.long_answer: Bernard–Soulier syndrome is caused by a quantitative or functional deficiency of the platelet membrane glycoprotein complex GPIb-IX-V (most commonly the GPIbα subunit). This complex is the principal platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor (vWF). vWF is synthesized and stored predominantly in vascular endothelial cells (a specialized form of epithelium) and in megakaryocytes/platelets. Thus, the syndrome indeed results from lack of a protein (GPIb) whose normal role is to bind a molecule (vWF) produced by epithelial-derived endothelial cells, leading to defective platelet adhesion and a bleeding tendency.

720129.long_answer: Ectopia cordis is a rare, usually lethal congenital malformation in which failure of midline mesoderm and ventral body-wall fusion during early embryogenesis leaves a defect through which the heart develops partly or completely outside the thoracic cavity. Because the heart lacks normal sternal and pericardial protection, severe cardiorespiratory compromise and infection typically occur, making the condition life-threatening shortly after birth.

612578.long_answer: Type 2A Megalencephalic Leukoencephalopathy is caused by recessive mutations in the HEPACAM (GlialCAM) gene. The canonical human HEPACAM protein consists of 416 amino acids, comprising two extracellular immunoglobulin-like domains, a single transmembrane segment, and a short cytoplasmic tail.
